No real money is involved. Learn order mechanics, portfolio tracking, and risk concepts across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What TradeHQ actually is TradeHQ is a free paper-trading simulator for people learning how markets work. Every account starts with $100,000 in virtual cash. Nothing on the site touches real money: there is no brokerage account, no deposit, no withdrawal and no order ever reaches an exchange. Supported holdings use periodically refreshed provider quotes. Unsupported assets can use fixed simulator prices, and charts may show synthetic practice candles. Price and chart labels explain their source and freshness. A practice account lets you examine decisions without putting savings at risk. For example, compare how different quantities change a hypothetical loss, or record why you changed an exit plan. These exercises do not establish why most beginners lose money or guarantee that practice changes later behaviour. What you can do here Paper trade 170 instruments across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities using market orders. Track a full practice portfolio — open positions, realised and unrealised P&L, maximum drawdown, open-position P&L dispersion and allocation snapshots. Explore four bundled course tracks (options, futures, macroeconomics and decision behaviour) and additional approved catalog releases, with quizzes and completion badges. Read a 49-term trading glossary written in plain language, each entry with a detailed explanation and a worked example. Follow step-by-step guides for individual assets, side-by-side asset comparisons, and named strategy walkthroughs. Keep a trading journal, build daily streaks with the daily challenge, and run a 30-day practice duel against a friend. Who it is for, and who it is not for TradeHQ is built for beginners and self-directed learners who want a place to rehearse market mechanics and a repeatable process without using real money. It can also be useful in classroom or independent-study settings. It is not for you if you want signals, copy-trading, portfolio management, or someone to tell you what to buy. We do not publish price targets, we do not run a Discord with calls, and we do not accept payment for coverage of any asset. If you are looking for a recommendation, this is the wrong site. Ways to begin learning Open the markets page and pick one instrument you already recognise. Read its available educational notes and distinguish identified facts from hypotheses about price changes. Compare fictional quantities and price changes to understand their effect on a virtual account. Record the assumptions and limitations of the selected worksheet. Review what the example illustrates at a time that suits your schedule; no transaction is required. What educational simulation can and cannot show Fictional examples can explain market mechanics without requiring a real transaction. Practice does not guarantee profit or replace independent education. A beginner can practice buying and selling holdings with virtual capital, then review those decisions without risking savings. TradeHQ currently supports market orders only; it does not simulate resting limit orders or short positions. A simulator does not reproduce the financial or personal consequences of a real loss. A written record can support review, but no pattern of participation establishes the quality of future decisions. Common questions Is TradeHQ free? Yes, entirely. There is no paid tier, no trial and no card required. Do I need an account? No. Practice trading, courses and the glossary work without signing up. An optional account supports profiles and community features. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore across devices when available; earlier guest trade history and journals remain on the original browser, while signed-in lessons and journey progress can sync privately when online. Is the money real? No. Every balance, order and result is simulated, and the platform holds no funds. Are the prices real? Supported assets use periodically refreshed provider observations. Unsupported assets can use fixed simulator prices; charts may be synthetic. Check each source and timestamp rather than assuming a continuous exchange feed. Does TradeHQ execute investments or provide personalized advice? No. Trading examples and educational indicator labels are illustrative, not personal recommendations, and the simulator places virtual orders only. Where is my data? Guest practice records stay in your browser. Signed-in cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored in Supabase and restored when the service is available. Guest trade history, journal entries and streaks remain browser-held; signed-in lessons and journey progress can sync privately. A badge count alone is not the complete course record. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. This page uses generated display data for education, not live market observations. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What is on the markets page The markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return. The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision. How to choose what to practise first Start with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent. The generated list cannot measure actual liquidity or spreads; study those concepts separately using dated reference material. Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence. Use the linked educational notes to distinguish an instrument's definition from uncertain explanations of price changes. Asset classes explained briefly Stocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates. ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk. Crypto: digital assets traded on venues with varying operating schedules, liquidity and risks. No fixed volatility or price relationship is implied. Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; central-bank announcements, economic data and other conditions are possible research topics. Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences. Reading a market list without being misled A percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range. Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event. Things that trip beginners on a markets screen Assuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry. Assuming a low nominal price alone establishes whether an asset is inexpensive; the units and method of valuation matter. Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks. Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity. pages.content: Practice Portfolio Learning notes: Practice Portfolio Review simulated positions, trades, P&L, drawdown and allocation snapshots. Guest records stay in your browser; account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore when the service is available. Server-recorded account trades restore across devices; earlier guest history and journals remain browser-held. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What the practice portfolio tracks The portfolio page shows open positions with entry prices, current practice prices and unrealised profit or loss, plus eligible recorded transaction history. Guest records live in local storage. Signed-in cash, positions and server-recorded transactions can restore when the service is available; clearing browser data does not delete that account copy. Earlier guest records and journals remain browser-held. Beyond raw P&L, the page calculates fee-inclusive closed-result win rate, average win versus average loss, current open-position return dispersion, and practice maximum drawdown. These summarize recorded outcomes and exposures that can help you review your practice process. The chart can include generated history; it is not a verified sequence of account observations. How to read your own numbers honestly Compare win rate, average realized win, average realized loss and costs together. A high win rate alone does not establish a positive result. Maximum drawdown describes a selected peak-to-trough decline. It does not measure every risk or predict your response to a real loss. A short run is an observation, not proof of a repeatable advantage. Selection, dependence, costs and changing conditions matter; no fixed trade count establishes an edge. If one position contributes most of a measured result, that observation alone cannot establish the effect of a method. Why results here do not transfer one-to-one The simulator applies a 0.1% practice transaction fee, rather than a real broker fee schedule. It does not model financing costs, taxes or actual market execution. Review practice results alongside these limits; they do not predict real-money results. The metrics explained in plain language Unrealised P&L: the difference between an open position's current marked value and its cost basis. Closing a position records realised P&L using its actual recorded proceeds and cost basis, which can differ from the earlier mark. All balances and results here remain virtual. Realised P&L: the result of trades you have actually closed. It is an accounting result, not a measure of decision quality. Open positions in profit: the share of current open positions showing positive unrealised P&L. This is not a closed-trade win rate. Open-position P&L dispersion: the spread of current position returns around their average. This is a snapshot, not a Sharpe ratio or time-series volatility measure. Practice maximum drawdown: the largest fall from a peak in locally stored snapshots, which can include generated hourly backfill. It is not an observed market record or proof that a strategy is survivable. Reviewing the portfolio weekly Choose a repeatable review interval for virtual results and compare the information recorded before each order with what became known later. A loss alone cannot establish whether the original reasoning was sound. Compare the largest virtual gain with its position size, price change, quotation source and costs. A large one-off outcome does not by itself establish skill or predict a similar future result. pages.content: Your First Virtual Trade, Explained Learning notes: Your First Virtual Trade, Explained Try an optional Daily Practice scenario, then follow five guided steps to understand an order, place a voluntary simulated trade, review cash and holdings, reflect, and choose what to learn next. No account or real money is required. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Step 1 — Understand an order before placing one The optional Daily Practice scenario comes first. In the guided lesson that follows, compare a displayed quote with the execution price. Consider two fictional shares showing $50 each. Their quoted purchase value is $100, and a 0.1% simulated fee adds $0.10. The estimated debit is therefore $100.10, assuming a $50 fill. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's Investor.gov guidance explains that a real market order's execution price is not guaranteed by the last quote. The simulator is simpler, and must not be mistaken for a live brokerage. The learner answers a short understanding check before entering the trading desk. The exercise presents an invented scenario for reading costs and uncertainty, not a stock recommendation or a return promise. Steps 2 and 3 — Place a voluntary virtual trade, then inspect the numbers Before opening the main virtual trading terminal, learners can optionally try a five-round fictional Practice Arena warm-up covering cash, holdings and a model fee. The warm-up's invented prices and browser-local balances are separate from the $100,000 trading portfolio, do not enter leaderboards, and do not advance the five-step journey. It can be skipped at any time; an Arena completion is not a saved guided trade. The guided link opens the normal virtual trading terminal, optionally selecting an illustrative asset. It never places an order on the learner's behalf. The visitor chooses a quantity and explicitly confirms any simulated transaction. A successful saved trade advances the journey; merely pressing a guide button does not. The next stage reads the learner's actual saved practice data. It shows remaining virtual cash, total account value, number of holdings, and the chosen trade's quantity, execution price, calculated fee and cash movement. Open-position returns change with the available reference price and are not guaranteed cash profits. A refreshed or delayed quote can differ from an earlier reference. Steps 4 and 5 — Reflect and return for daily practice Learners write a private reflection explaining what surprised them about the price or fee and what they will check before another exercise. New reflection text stays in the browser even when signed in. Only the completed step can sync with the account. Older reflections that already synced remain private. TradeHQ then recommends a risk-management lesson and the existing Daily Practice exercises; completion does not certify readiness to risk real money. The journey records completed steps in browser storage so guest visitors can return later on the same browser. Signed-in members can also privately sync supported lessons, quiz drafts, reading position and journey progress between devices when online. A course's most-recent-lesson record helps resume the right lesson. Clearing guest browser data can remove that guest's progress; portfolio backups do not include learning records. What a first practice result can and cannot show A fictional profit or loss is useful for checking arithmetic, exposure, and whether the learner understood their own decision. It does not reproduce real transaction liquidity, bid/ask spreads, slippage, tax obligations or the consequences of risking money. A short winning streak is not evidence of an investing skill. The intended result of this lesson is a better explanation of the order and its limitations, not a trade signal. pages.content: Beginner Trading Practice Guide Learning notes: Beginner Trading Practice Guide An introduction to the virtual practice dashboard, order mechanics and a worked buy/sell-fee example. Links to longer courses and reference material; $100,000 is simulated money, not an investment account. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What this page actually provides This page is a starting map and interactive practice dashboard, not a complete textbook or independently tested trading course. It introduces quote reading, simulated market orders, fees and reviewing hypothetical outcomes. Use the linked structured courses for deeper explanations of instruments, order types and portfolio concepts. The exercises illustrate arithmetic and questions to ask, not a profitable strategy. Four checks for a virtual practice exercise Exposure: quantify the share of virtual cash used and calculate what a chosen adverse price change would do to the holding. Exit assumptions: write down both a higher and a lower hypothetical sale price. TradeHQ does not support resting limit or stop orders. Observation quality: record the quote source, timestamp, asset and quote currency. A generated chart need not reproduce traded market history. Review: retain the original assumptions, both virtual fees and alternative outcomes. One or ten practice results do not establish a repeatable advantage. Worked example: virtual shares, fees and two outcomes Assume a purely hypothetical purchase of ten shares at $50 each. The gross cost is $500 and a 0.1% virtual purchase fee is $0.50, so the total cash used is $500.50. If the assumed sale price is $46, the gross proceeds are $460 and a 0.1% virtual sale fee is $0.46; net proceeds are $459.54. Compared with the original $500.50 cost, the round trip produces a loss of $40.96. For the same ten shares, a separate hypothetical sale at $54 yields $540 gross, less a $0.54 virtual sale fee, or $539.46 net. Subtract the $500.50 initial cost to get a gain of $38.96. These prices are invented, not a forecast or observed fills. Actual transactions can involve spreads, slippage, taxes and other costs not captured here. What this simulator cannot teach by itself TradeHQ offers virtual market orders, not real brokerage transactions, short positions or resting limit/stop orders. Even when a displayed quote comes from an external provider, a simulated fill does not establish that the same price or liquidity would be available on an exchange. Use the structured courses and linked sources to check concepts rather than treating a synthetic sentiment label, an indicator, or a hypothetical growth calculator as a verified trading signal. Practice outcomes do not predict real-money results. The vocabulary you need before anything else Bid and ask: at a given time, the best displayed bid and ask are quoted buying and selling prices. Their difference is the spread. Actual fills and costs can differ from that snapshot. Liquidity: the availability of buyers and sellers at prices and quantities. Limited liquidity can make a real order harder or more costly to execute. Volatility: a measure of price variation over a stated period. It describes past movement; it cannot dictate one universally appropriate exit level or position size. Leverage: exposure larger than posted funds through borrowing or derivatives. Gains and losses can be magnified, and collateral or liquidation rules vary by product and venue. TradeHQ does not provide leverage. Expectancy example, not a forecast: five hypothetical wins of $30 and five losses of $20 total $50 before costs. Ten $2 round-trip fees reduce that to $30 net. This invented ten-trade record is too small and artificial to establish a repeatable advantage. A first-month plan Week one: label the bid, ask, spread and quote time on an example, then inspect virtual market orders without using real funds. Week two: write assumptions before a virtual example, including quantity, fee, possible lower sale price and an alternative outcome. Week three: check each recorded virtual outcome against its original assumptions; distinguish a mark from an executable real-world quote. Week four: compare the journal entries for missing costs, changed assumptions and hindsight bias. Note what the simulation cannot test. Answers stay on this browser. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. How the daily challenge works Daily offers a quick hypothetical market scenario alongside a longer ten-question case study. You choose a response, compare the reasoning and trade-offs, then answer a short bonus knowledge question about market basics. Completing the quick reasoning step or all ten case-study questions advances the browser-stored streak at most once per local day. Directional reflections are not forecast scores. The scenario's prices, news events and dates are exercise inputs, not a report of what happened in today's markets. Choosing long, short or hold records a reflection; it does not place an order. Use the explanation to compare assumptions and uncertainty rather than treating completion as evidence of forecasting skill. Using a daily habit to support review Review the reasoning and arithmetic when it is useful; no particular frequency establishes skill. A short exercise is optional. Choose a study interval that fits your schedule. A streak counts participation; it does not establish that a particular study habit has formed. After a missed day, resume when your schedule allows; a streak is a participation aid, not a skill grade. A longer daily practice session The deeper exercise develops one case across ten linked questions, so the learner can calculate an input, interpret the result and identify a limitation. Topics rotate between portfolio arithmetic, transaction costs and supported orders, price-data freshness, risk and uncertainty, and decision habits. The visuals show selected hypothetical inputs with numeric labels; they are not live market charts. Worked explanations appear after each submitted answer, including when the answer was wrong. After you finish, the case takeaway provides a review guide for checking the reasoning. Checked answers are saved on this browser. After the first saved answer, the case keeps its own snapshot if a new bank is approved while you are working. Clearing site data removes this local history; an account does not synchronize this case history to another device. The configured generation workflow targets a new 50-exercise bank every two calendar months in five parts using the configured Gemini API. A target schedule is not a publication guarantee. Each completed bank remains private and editable in the owner’s admin panel until final review and approval. If generation hits a quota limit, fails validation or awaits review, the approved bank continues rotating. Fifty exercises can therefore repeat before the next bank begins; revisits are review practice rather than a claim of brand-new daily content. The feature does not use a paid provider fallback. What the challenges cover A hypothetical market scenario with stated exercise inputs, rather than current market news. Comparing long, short and hold reasoning without grading one market direction as objectively correct. A bank of 50 deeper exercises, each with a substantial hypothetical case, a labelled visual and ten linked questions with worked explanations. The existing short bonus quiz plus a case takeaway with a review guide. How the streak is counted A streak advances once per calendar day in your own local time zone, so completing a challenge late one evening and early the next morning still counts as two consecutive days. The counter lives in your browser, which means clearing site data resets it and using a different device starts a separate count even when you have an account; sign-in does not back up local streaks. There is no penalty for missing a day beyond the counter resetting, and longer streaks unlock browser-local completion badges, not prizes or qualifications. Nothing about the challenge involves money, prizes or entry fees. If you miss a day Nothing bad happens beyond the counter going back to one. The purpose of the streak is to make practice frequent, not to punish a missed evening, and restarting after a gap is the normal experience rather than a failure. The counter is not a judgment about you or a measurement of future returns. If daily practice does not fit your schedule, choose a workable review rhythm. A record of what you learned is more informative than a raw session count. References and related pages Practice desk Glossary Challenge a friend Educational simulation only — not financial advice. pages.title: Practice Arena — Interactive Virtual Trading Decisions | TradeHQ
pages.description: Practise five fictional trading decisions in minutes. Reveal price changes, see virtual cash and fees, and review your reasoning. Free, private, no signup.
pages.content: TradeHQ Practice Arena Learning notes: TradeHQ Practice Arena Practice Arena is a free, self-contained interactive training exercise. Choose a beginner or intermediate scenario, observe deliberately fictional prices, and decide whether to buy a small exercise position, sell already held units or wait. Each decision reveals another invented observation and explains the accounting and assumptions. The Arena begins with its own $10,000 fictional cash ledger. The model charges a 0.1% fee on virtual buys and sells, and records exercise choices privately in this browser. It never places an order on TradeHQ's normal virtual trading terminal, changes a user portfolio, alters a public leaderboard, or consults a real-market quote. A favorable exercise result cannot establish trading competence or forecast real performance. After reviewing a scenario, continue with the beginner journey, risk lesson or deeper Daily Practice. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. How Practice Arena works Practice Arena is an interactive training exercise built around deliberate choices rather than trading predictions. Choose one of three authored paths: Your First Decision, Size Changes Everything, or Stay With the Plan. Each path contains five small decision rounds. The next hypothetical observation is hidden until you choose to buy a fictional unit, sell units you already hold, or wait without making an order. This helps you practise noticing assumptions without claiming that a particular price direction is objectively correct. All instruments and prices in the Arena are invented classroom examples. They are not historical exchange observations, live quotes, market forecasts or recommendations to buy or sell any real security. A user can enter the exercise without an account, paying a fee or connecting a brokerage. The separate practice balance begins with 10,000 fictional dollars for the purposes of these specific decisions. This is not the main TradeHQ simulator's 100,000-dollar balance, and nothing in the Arena sends an order to the main trading terminal. A worked illustration of the virtual ledger Imagine a fictional asset displayed at $100 a unit, an exercise cash balance of $10,000 and an order to purchase one unit. The classroom calculation uses the purchase notional of $100 plus a 0.1% transaction fee of $0.10. Exercise cash becomes $9,899.90 and the held unit is initially worth $100 at the same fictional mark, leaving marked equity of $9,999.90. The decrease is the modelled fee, not the loss of the entire purchase value. If the next invented observation is $102, the one held unit is marked at $102 and the combined exercise equity would be $10,001.90. If a user simply observes instead of buying, no units are purchased or sold, cash stays unchanged and no transaction fee is charged. A sale is allowed only for units actually held; a user cannot open a short position in this teaching exercise. Costs and changes are displayed immediately after each decision. These examples describe arithmetic, not actual exchange settlement, liquidity, taxes or execution. Why the Arena asks for a reason Before revealing the next scenario observation, you may write what you are trying to test or why you would prefer to observe without placing an order. Afterward, the review panel compares the recorded action with the next invented mark, the modelled fee, remaining cash and the value of any held units. A profitable fictional decision is not declared a good decision, and an unprofitable one is not automatically described as a mistake. The purpose is to examine what is known, what was assumed and how the decision affects the ledger. The first path focuses on basic cash and fee accounting, the second on the dollar effect of position quantity, and the intermediate path on distinguishing evidence from unsupported claims under changing conditions. The next step can be an existing beginner journey, a risk-management lesson or a deeper Daily Practice case. The three paths are finite and can be repeated; TradeHQ does not advertise unlimited new historical market scenarios. After completing five rounds, the review separates the value effect of fictional price changes from the virtual fees charged for buying or selling. The price effect includes changes in units still held, so it is not necessarily a realized trading result. Learners can expand a chronological record of every decision and its optional stated reason, then write a private closing reflection about what to test again. This information remains on their device. The optional usefulness prompt lets a learner choose whether an exercise was useful, confusing or too easy. Choosing an option does not transmit it. If a learner explicitly opens the Contact page, TradeHQ can prefill an email draft that they may edit and decide whether to send. Selecting a usefulness response does not automatically submit the response. Separate performance and optional analytics requests are described in the Privacy Policy. Privacy, limitations and what the result means Arena exercises use intentionally fictional prices and an isolated local ledger. They never change the signed-in practice portfolio, guest simulator balance, public rankings or verified competition records. Decisions, optional notes and completion history stay in the same browser. Clearing site data may erase them, and signing in does not currently synchronize Arena sessions across devices. The exercise does not simulate market spreads, order-book depth, slippage, broker regulation, borrowing, stop execution, tax costs or the emotional consequences of risking real savings. A finished session is a record of educational participation, not investment advice, a skill certification, a personalized trading recommendation or evidence of likely real financial returns. Visitors can leave without making a trade. Waiting is a deliberate choice and carries no fictional transaction fee. Optional Arena usage milestones use Amplitude only after an adult visitor confirms they are at least 18 and explicitly accepts the renewed analytics choice; no prior acceptance is reused. Replay and automatic interactions are disabled in the website analytics setup. These events can indicate a start, completion, resume or later same-browser visit, but do not transmit decisions, balances, portfolio identities or written reflections. Rejecting analytics does not disable the simulator. A five-minute voluntary study offers before-and-after concept questions and optional feedback; the answers stay in the current page until the participant explicitly copies or prepares an email, and no message is sent automatically. A weekly lesson, delivered only if you want it The TradeHQ Newsletter is a free, optional educational email for readers who want to understand financial concepts one useful idea at a time. Each issue is designed to explain a beginner-friendly topic in plain language, with a specific example and an honest account of what the example does not show. The newsletter is intended as a separate educational resource; no TradeHQ account, brokerage account or real-money trade is necessary to read it. Issues are prepared through an editorial process and sent only after the owner has approved their content. Drafts are not automatically distributed. The intended frequency is one lesson per week, but provider outages, review delays or quota limits can interrupt the schedule. An email subscription is not a course enrolment and does not guarantee a new lesson on a particular date. What readers can expect A focused beginner-level explanation about topics such as order mechanics, portfolio accounting, market data, risk concepts and common assumptions. Concrete arithmetic or a worked hypothetical example when it helps clarify a concept, with its simplifications made explicit. Educational context instead of individual investment recommendations, price predictions, 'buy now' messages or promotions of a brokerage account. A free and optional subscription. How subscribing and unsubscribing work To request the newsletter, enter an email address and explicitly agree to receive the lessons. TradeHQ sends a confirmation link and a six-digit verification code to eligible addresses. The subscription is not active until the recipient confirms using either method. An unconfirmed email address is not placed into the confirmed delivery list. This double opt-in process is intended to reduce unwanted mail and accidental sign-ups. Every confirmed recipient can unsubscribe using the link in an email. The unsubscribe page does not require a TradeHQ account. Unsubscribing stops future educational mailings through this list; it does not erase an unrelated account or a browser-held virtual portfolio. Newsletter content cannot assess your finances, risk tolerance or suitability for a particular trade. Descriptions of historical events require their own checked sources and dates, while invented practice examples should never be treated as market history. Reading a lesson is not evidence of trading competence or a promise of investment returns. The best way to use an issue is to understand one idea, work through its example yourself and then practise the relevant concept in a clearly labelled fictional scenario or a voluntary virtual order. The Practice Arena and Daily Practice give you those options without asking you to risk real savings. pages.description: TradeHQ privacy policy covering guest browser data, signed-in portfolio sync, optional accounts, analytics, advertising and your choices.
pages.content: Privacy Policy Learning notes: Privacy Policy Guest simulator records stay in your browser. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored with Supabase; account, community and consented analytics features also involve provider processing. See the full policy for details. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Policy update Last Updated: November 22, 2026 Information TradeHQ Handles TradeHQ can be used without creating an account. The data handled depends on the features you choose. • Guest simulator data: practice cash, positions and trade history are stored in your browser with a separate browser-local recovery copy. You can download or explicitly restore a portable practice backup JSON file containing trading history and any private journal notes. The backup feature does not upload this file. Backup formats can be manually edited: TradeHQ validates file structure and arithmetic but does not certify authenticity, investment performance or leaderboard ranking. An imported guest file remains unverified. Guest learning-journey progress, course progress, streaks and related settings remain browser-stored. For signed-in users, lesson completion, unfinished quiz answers, reading position and first-trade journey progress may also be saved privately in Supabase and synchronized across devices when online. New beginner-journey reflection text stays on the device. Older reflections already synchronized remain private in the account. Streaks and unrelated browser preferences are not part of this account sync. • Signed-in portfolio data: Supabase stores account cash, positions and server-recorded practice orders, including asset, quantity, execution price, fees, time and simulated result. These account records restore across devices when the service is available. Signed-in users can also download a server-signed current-cycle historical practice export and verify its integrity against their authenticated account. This file may contain account identifiers and private transaction details; it is not publicly shared or accepted as an upload that replaces ranked trades. A first-time browser import stores cash and positions as an unranked portfolio; earlier guest trade history stays in its original browser. Starting a fresh ranked practice cycle archives the previous account snapshot privately. Journals remain browser-held; signed-in lesson and beginner-journey progress can sync privately and are not used to determine public trading ranks. • Optional account data: if you create an account, Supabase processes authentication data such as your email or provider identity and can store profile fields including username, country and bio. • Foundations assessments and certificates: when a signed-in learner uses the optional Foundations programme, Supabase stores account-linked assessment identifiers, scores, possible points and qualifying learning dates. When a learner requests a certificate, TradeHQ stores the recipient name they provide, the programme and milestone, template version, issue date and qualifying assessment evidence so the same certificate can be retrieved. Name corrections are retained as revision history; an earlier name is not erased simply by correcting it. Optional verification sharing stores a hash of the verification credential and its name revision. A person given a valid verification link can check the programme version, milestone and issue date, not the recipient name or private scores. The learner can withdraw or replace the verification link; correcting the name invalidates the previous link. Account deletion cascades to these account-linked Foundations records. A downloaded PDF or copy shared outside TradeHQ is not removed by withdrawing verification or deleting an account. • Community data: signed-in features can store selected practice statistics, public-profile settings, reviews and duel/challenge records. A separate setting, OFF by default, lets a member voluntarily disclose up to 20 current-cycle server-recorded simulated trade entries on an otherwise public profile: asset, buy/sell, quantity, execution price, fee and date. The public data response also includes trade total, simulated realised profit/loss where recorded, and price-source information, even when a visible profile row shows fewer fields. Private journals, reflections, past cycles and browser-only records are never shared by this feature. These are simulated results, not brokerage statements or verified real-money performance. Creating or joining a practice duel requires public profiles. Eligible public duel responses include participant identifiers, invite code, recorded starting values, score values and relevant dates; other visitors may read them while the applicable profiles are public. Switching a profile to private restricts new non-participant access under the duel access policy; participants can retain access, and previously viewed copies cannot be recalled. • Review submissions and interactions: TradeHQ stores your submitted display name (if provided), review text, rating, moderation status and an IP-derived hash used for duplicate prevention. The hash is restricted to authorized backend processing; it is not a public review field. A hash is not necessarily anonymous information. Likes are stored with your account ID and the review ID to enforce one like per account. Public pages show totals, not individual liker identities. Owner replies are public. Reviews removed from public view remain in the private admin panel for restoration. Contact TradeHQ for privacy or removal requests. • Optional TradeHQ Newsletter: if you explicitly request the educational newsletter, TradeHQ stores your email address, consent/confirmation status, the date and source of signup, unsubscribe status, and delivery receipts in private Supabase records. Resend handles email delivery and receives your address for confirmations and issues. We never add prior contact records to the mailing list without permission. Every newsletter provides an unsubscribe link, and you may use the contact page to request deletion. • Contact messages: by default the contact page opens your email app or lets you copy a draft into webmail. If the optional direct-send service is configured, Cloudflare Turnstile processes challenge and connection information and Resend processes the message, sender reply address and recipient information to deliver it to the maintainer's inbox. TradeHQ does not retain direct-send message bodies in its application database. The maintainer's email provider retains delivered messages according to its settings. • Technical data: hosting, authentication, security and abuse-prevention services can receive normal request information such as IP address, browser/device information and server logs. • Website performance: current pages load Cloudflare Web Analytics to measure page loading and performance. Its browser beacon can send the page URL, a page-load identifier, timing and browser performance measurements to Cloudflare, separately from optional Amplitude events. These performance requests can run before an analytics choice and after Amplitude is rejected. Cloudflare states that its Web Analytics usage metrics do not use cookies, local storage or fingerprinting to track individuals. This does not mean that network requests contain no connection information or that every jurisdiction exempts this processing from privacy requirements. • Font delivery: pages request stylesheets and font files from Google Fonts. Google receives the connecting IP address, the requested resource URL and request headers, which can include browser/operating-system information and the referring page according to browser settings. These requests are separate from Amplitude consent and may occur before a choice or after rejection. Google states that its Fonts API does not set or log cookies and does not use Fonts information to create end-user profiles or for targeted advertising. • Optional analytics and advertising data: TradeHQ offers a newly scoped analytics choice only to visitors affirmatively confirming they are at least 18. This confirmation is for optional analytics; it is not an age restriction on lessons, guest practice or sign-in. Visitors under 18 should reject optional analytics. If accepted, Amplitude can receive limited Practice Arena milestone events and two leaderboard registration-flow events (an eligible signed-out leaderboard visit, and a newly created account subsequently authenticated in that same browser within seven days), along with its pseudonymous browser identity and ordinary network metadata. The two leaderboard custom events contain no email, account ID, username, profile details, portfolio data, transaction information, or form content. The temporary seven-day same-browser attribution marker stores only a visit timestamp and is cleared on consent rejection or successful attribution. No custom Amplitude events are sent when optional analytics is declined; the website does not claim visitor identity is anonymous. Amplitude's automatic page, click, form, network and attribution collection and session replay are disabled; the two explicitly triggered attribution events are the only leaderboard funnel measurement. Earlier v1/v2 analytics permissions are not reused. Google AdSense has separate advertising choices and may use cookies or similar identifiers for ad delivery, measurement and, where applicable, personalisation. • Practice Arena research: exercise decisions, private written reasons, closing reflections and history stay in your browser and are not automatically submitted to a research database. An optional, adult-only research questionnaire keeps answers on the open page and only prepares an email if you deliberately choose to do so; you must send that email yourself. Sending an email reveals your sender address and may include other email-provider metadata. Answers are not anonymous once linked with a sender or identifying comments. If you accept Amplitude analytics, TradeHQ may record Arena view/start/finish/resume milestones, scenario ID and difficulty, and whether this browser returned on a later day. Custom Arena events do not include trading choices, portfolio values, account IDs, written notes or questionnaire answers. This opt-in measurement uses the existing Amplitude service's consented visitor identity; it does not create a separate TradeHQ research identifier. Declining analytics disables those custom milestones. A same-browser return event does not prove a person learned or voluntarily returned. TradeHQ does not require a payment card, bank account or brokerage account to place simulated trades. How Information Is Used TradeHQ uses data only for the feature that needs it: operating the simulator, authenticating optional accounts, showing profile/community features, preventing abuse, responding to messages, delivering a voluntarily confirmed TradeHQ Newsletter subscription, diagnosing problems and improving the service. Amplitude is used for limited, explicitly triggered Arena and leaderboard-to-new-account registration analytics after renewed adult opt-in. TradeHQ measures only consenting eligible visitors and same-browser new-account confirmations within seven days; email-link confirmations in another browser and visitors who reject analytics are not included, so any conversion rate is an incomplete proxy, not a claim about all visitors. pages.description: A short squeeze occurs when a rising price or difficulty borrowing a security puts pressure on short sellers to close positions by buying shares.
pages.content: Short Squeeze — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Short Squeeze — Trading Wiki A short squeeze occurs when a rising price or difficulty borrowing a security puts pressure on short sellers to close positions by buying shares. That covering demand can add further upward pressure to the price. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. Limited source check: 2026-11-01. Checked short-sale closing mechanics, periodic short-interest snapshots, the days-to-cover formula and 10 × ($28 − $20) = $80 illustrative loss against FINRA sources. No individual squeeze event, predictive signal or historical return series was verified. This is not independent professional review. In depth A short seller borrows a security, sells it, and later needs to buy equivalent securities to close the position and return what was borrowed. If the price rises instead of falling, the short position loses value. A short squeeze can develop when price increases or borrowing constraints cause multiple short sellers to cover at the same time; those purchases add demand and can intensify the upward move. Short interest is one useful measure of outstanding short positions, while days to cover compares reported short interest with average daily share volume. FINRA publishes these measures as market data, but they do not create a universal squeeze threshold or a reliable timing signal. Reported short interest is also a periodic snapshot rather than a real-time count. Borrowing availability, trading volume, price movement, liquidity and the behaviour of market participants can all affect whether heavy short positioning ever becomes a squeeze. Key points A squeeze can occur when rising prices or borrowing pressure cause short sellers to cover Covering purchases can add further upward pressure to the price Short interest and days to cover provide context but do not define a universal squeeze threshold Why it matters when you are learning Treat short interest and days-to-cover figures as context, not a trigger. Compare current reported data with earlier periods and check how the price and trading volume are behaving; no single percentage or ratio guarantees that a squeeze will occur. Worked exercise and its limits Hypothetical short-sale worksheet: 10 borrowed shares sold at $20 and repurchased at $28 create an $80 loss before borrowing costs. Explain why buying to cover adds demand, while a price rise alone cannot reveal who bought. TradeHQ cannot open short positions. In depth Standard RSI compares smoothed upward and downward price changes over a selected lookback and expresses their relative strength on a 0–100 scale. A divergence compares its selected swings with price swings: for example, a lower price low alongside a higher RSI low. Those observations can occur before either a reversal or continued decline. Changing the interval or which swings count changes the comparison. No timeframe is established here as reliably predictive. Use matching external price and standard RSI data for the worksheet; the RSI-style value in TradeHQ is not a standard historical RSI calculation. Key points Bullish divergence: price lower low + RSI higher low Bearish divergence: price higher high + RSI lower high Results depend on the sample and settings; no reliable timeframe is established here Why it matters when you are learning Compare the price swings and RSI swings over the same dates and settings. Record both divergences followed by reversals and those followed by continuation; divergence is not an entry guarantee. Worked exercise and its limits Invent two observations from one matching interval: at A, price is $100 and standard RSI is 25; at B, price is $95 and RSI is 32. Price makes a lower low while RSI makes a higher low, so these stipulated swings show bullish divergence. The RSI values are given inputs, not values calculated from just these two prices. Extend the price path once to $105 and separately to $85: the same divergence can precede either outcome. TradeHQ’s RSI-style display is not a standard historical RSI series. In depth Bollinger Bands place upper and lower bands around a moving average using a selected measure of price dispersion. A commonly used setup is a 20-period simple average with bands two standard deviations away, but settings vary. A squeeze describes relatively narrow bands compared with a stated lookback. It does not establish when volatility will increase, which direction price will move or how far. Past price distributions need not be normal, and the bands are not a guaranteed probability interval. Record the calculation and comparison period before evaluating later candles; avoid choosing a squeeze only after seeing a large move. Key points Narrow bands describe lower recent volatility; they do not establish when a breakout will occur A break outside a band is an observation that can continue or reverse Volume provides another observation, without validating a future move Why it matters when you are learning Compare the bandwidth over a stated sample. In depth A Fair Value Gap (FVG) is a three-candle chart label used in Smart Money Concepts (SMC) and Inner Circle Trader (ICT) frameworks. For an upward example, candle one’s high is below candle three’s low; for a downward example, candle one’s low is above candle three’s high. The marked range depends on the selected candles, interval and data source. It does not establish economic fair value, a market-efficiency violation, unfilled orders or the identity and intentions of participants. To study it, freeze the selection rules before inspecting later prices and record both revisited and unvisited ranges. Neither a longer candle interval, accompanying volume nor overlapping chart labels establishes a measured chance of a revisit or a profitable entry. Use the invented worksheet below to compare two possible later paths without treating either as a forecast. Key points A selected three-candle sequence with non-overlapping first and third price ranges Labels a non-overlapping candle range that need not be revisited Not a validated entry rule or guarantee that a gap will fill Why it matters when you are learning Identify the three candles and the non-overlapping price range. Compare examples where price revisits the range with examples where it does not; a gap need not fill or act as support. Worked exercise and its limits Invent three candles where the first high is $100 and the third low is $102. Mark the $100–$102 non-overlap. Then draw a path that revisits it and one that never does. Neither proves unfilled orders or economic fair value. In depth A bull trap is a retrospective label for a price move above a selected resistance area that subsequently reverses below it. The apparent breakout can encourage purchases, but a chart alone cannot establish buyers’ motives or a deliberate attempt to trap them. In depth Whale is informal language for a participant or wallet with a large position. Holding or moving a large amount does not by itself establish manipulation. Spoofing involves deceptive orders intended to be cancelled rather than executed; wash-trading allegations concern transactions creating a false appearance of activity. Proving either requires evidence beyond a candlestick, displayed order or wallet transfer and depends on applicable rules. A transfer may reflect custody reorganization or another purpose unrelated to a market sale. Distinguish observable size and timing from claims about ownership, intent and price effects. Do not present alleged misconduct as a validated trading signal. In depth Support and resistance describe price areas selected from earlier reactions or other chart rules. A past low can be used to mark support and a past high resistance, but subsequent transactions can occur beyond either. A level’s appearance depends on data frequency, adjustment, chosen tolerance and how many observations are counted. A level marked on a daily chart is not automatically more predictive than one on a shorter interval. Specify the rule before inspecting later prices, record breaks and state whether a purported reaction is an intraday observation or a close. The drawing is a description, not evidence of hidden demand or a guaranteed exit. Key points Support and resistance label areas of prior reactions rather than floors or ceilings Some chart frameworks relabel a crossed level; the next reaction remains uncertain Record the selected touches, interval and volume without ranking a level as reliably strongest Why it matters when you are learning Draw zones from specified price observations and compare alternative anchors. These are chart descriptions rather than floors, ceilings or a required first trading method. Worked exercise and its limits State how close prices must be to count as a touch, then mark a zone using only earlier candles. Keep later breaks in the record. Changing the zone after seeing an outcome makes the exercise vulnerable to hindsight bias. pages.title: Head and Shoulders — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: A head and shoulders pattern has three peaks, with a higher central peak and two lower shoulders.
pages.content: Head and Shoulders — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Head and Shoulders — Trading Wiki A head and shoulders pattern has three peaks, with a higher central peak and two lower shoulders. A neckline connects the intervening lows; breaking it is a chart observation, not a confirmed future decline or guaranteed target. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth The head and shoulders pattern is a commonly described reversal formation in technical analysis. It consists of three distinct peaks: a left shoulder, a higher central peak (the head), and a right shoulder that is approximately equal in height to the left shoulder. The troughs between these peaks are connected by a line called the neckline, and a break below this neckline completes the conventional pattern description; continued decline is a hypothesis that can fail. The conventional description follows five price phases; these observations do not establish participant motives. Phase one: the market trends upward and creates the left shoulder, a normal swing high. Phase two: a pullback creates the first neckline touch. Phase three: renewed buying pushes price to a higher high (the head), recording a higher observed peak, without establishing acceleration or future direction. Phase four: another pullback returns to the neckline area, and bulls attempt one more push higher. Phase five: the rally fails to reach the head's height, forming the right shoulder — a lower peak that some analysts interpret as weakening upward momentum. The measured move technique provides a price target: measure the vertical distance from the head to the neckline, then subtract that distance from the neckline breakout point. Volume adds a separate historical observation; it does not validate a forecast. Some descriptions compare volume across the shoulders, head and neckline break. State the observation window and volume source; a lower volume does not by itself establish participants’ conviction or predict the next move. Volume alone does not establish the probability that a neckline break will persist. The inverse pattern uses three troughs rather than peaks and is commonly interpreted as a bullish hypothesis, which can fail. Key points Three peaks: left shoulder, head (highest), right shoulder A neckline break describes the chart; a measured target is a projection, not a guaranteed outcome The inverse shape can occur without a lasting upward reversal Why it matters when you are learning Draw the three peaks and neckline, then distinguish the pattern's measured-move convention from the actual later price. A projected target is a hypothesis rather than an expected payout. Worked exercise and its limits Mark three hypothetical peaks at $50, $55 and $51 with intervening lows near $46. If you project the $9 head-to-neckline height below $46, the arithmetic target is $37. It is a projection that price need not reach. pages.description: A double bottom is a W-shaped chart pattern with two troughs near a similar level.
pages.content: Double Bottom — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Double Bottom — Trading Wiki A double bottom is a W-shaped chart pattern with two troughs near a similar level. A later move above the intervening peak fits the pattern, but does not ensure that a rally continues. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth The double bottom is a bullish reversal pattern that forms after a sustained downtrend, characterized by two consecutive troughs at approximately the same price level separated by a moderate peak (the neckline). The pattern resembles the letter 'W' on a chart and is commonly interpreted as a possible reversal near a repeated price low; the chart alone cannot establish that selling pressure has been exhausted. The conventional description records a sequence of price observations. The first bottom forms as the existing downtrend reaches a point where buyers emerge, creating a bounce. The subsequent rally creates the neckline — the intermediate peak between the two bottoms. However, the rally loses momentum and price declines again to retest the support level established by the first bottom. The second bottom is the critical test: if price rises again from the low, it records another bounce at that level without proving the cause or durability. In the conventional chart description, a later move above the intervening peak completes the pattern; it does not confirm a lasting reversal. The measured move target equals the depth of the pattern — the distance from the bottoms to the neckline — projected upward from the neckline breakout point. Volume characteristics provide context but do not establish predictive reliability. Some descriptions compare volume during the two declines and the neckline break. Lower reported volume is an observation, not proof of reduced selling conviction or a future rebound. A volume observation does not establish a measured breakout failure rate. RSI divergence is another description of the selected historical data, not evidence of a dramatically higher success rate. If the RSI makes a higher low while price makes an equal or lower low at the second bottom, the oscillator reading is higher than at the earlier low; this does not validate a subsequent reversal. Key points W-shaped pattern with two tests of the same support level A later move above the middle peak completes the conventional description, not a confirmed forecast RSI divergence is another historical observation, not independent proof of a profitable reversal Why it matters when you are learning Identify the two lows and the intervening high under fixed rules, including failed examples. A familiar pattern does not establish a beginner’s readiness or confidence level. Worked exercise and its limits Draw troughs near $30 separated by a $35 high. The $5 height gives a conventional projection of $40 after a break above $35, but the next move could reverse. State the tolerance used to call the troughs similar. pages.title: Limit Order vs Market Order — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: Market orders seek prompt execution at available prices.
pages.content: Limit Order vs Market Order — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Limit Order vs Market Order — Trading Wiki Market orders seek prompt execution at available prices. Limit orders set a price boundary and may remain unfilled. Choosing an order type involves a trade-off between execution priority and price control. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth A market order requests execution at available prices without setting a maximum buy or minimum sell price. A limit order sets that boundary, but may fill partly or not at all. A last-traded price is not a commitment that the same quantity is available now. For a hypothetical example, suppose the ask shows $20 for only five shares while a buyer wants ten. A market fill may reach higher offers. A $20 buy limit cannot execute above $20, but the unfilled quantity may remain open or expire according to its instructions. A stop-market instruction, by contrast, becomes a market order after its trigger and does not promise the trigger price. Compare prices, completion, delays and modeled costs separately rather than assume an order type ensures better financial results. TradeHQ supports simplified virtual market orders only; it does not operate an exchange order book or pending orders. Key points Market orders request execution at available prices; fills and price depend on liquidity Limit orders: a price boundary, not an exact fill price; they may remain unfilled Limit prices constrain execution price, without ensuring a fill or preventing loss Why it matters when you are learning Compare price control with execution uncertainty. A market order prioritises execution at available prices; a limit order sets a price boundary but may not fill. TradeHQ currently executes market practice orders only. Worked exercise and its limits Suppose a quoted ask is $10 but the next available fill is $10.20. A market purchase may fill at $10.20; a $10 buy limit cannot fill above its limit and may remain unfilled. TradeHQ supports market orders only. pages.content: Stop Loss Hunting — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Stop Loss Hunting — Trading Wiki A suspected intentional move through levels where stop orders may be placed. A price reversal alone does not prove manipulation, identify a trader or reveal actual order locations. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Stop loss hunting is a term used for a suspected intentional move through levels where stop orders may be placed. A chart showing a move through such a level does not establish manipulation, the identity of a trader or actual order locations. Distinguish a suspected explanation from observable prices, actual order records and findings by a market authority; similar chart movements can have different causes. In a hypothetical example, several participants could choose exits below a recent low. If the market trades through those levels, triggered sell orders could add to selling pressure. That example describes a possible order-flow mechanism, rather than evidence that actual orders were concentrated there or that another participant deliberately moved the price. A later reversal could reflect new orders, changing liquidity, news or other causes. A wick records an interval's price range; it is not a visual signature proving a completed hunt. Public order books show displayed orders, while stop instructions, hidden orders and positions may not be publicly visible. Liquidation estimates and third-party heatmaps also require a clearly identified data source and methodology; they do not reveal every account or the location of the next price move. Charts aggregate trades over a chosen interval, so changing the interval can change how an apparent sweep looks. To examine a suspected event, first record the instrument, venue, observation time, price and volume data. Separate that record from assumptions about hidden orders or participant intent. Compare other plausible explanations and avoid treating a single chart pattern as proof. Trading safeguards involve trade-offs. A stop-market instruction can execute at a different price from its trigger, a stop-limit instruction can remain unfilled, and an unsubmitted mental exit is not an exchange order. Changing a stop level or using a time-based exit cannot guarantee protection against loss or an adverse move. TradeHQ's simulator currently supports market practice orders rather than automated stops. Its displayed practice charts should not be treated as forensic evidence about actual exchange manipulation. Key points Describes a suspected mechanism, rather than proving actual stop locations A reversal after a level breaks does not establish deliberate manipulation No stop buffer or exit method guarantees protection against loss Why it matters when you are learning A stop can be triggered before price reverses for many ordinary reasons, including volatility, clustered order flow, spread changes, and the level you chose. Avoid assuming manipulation without evidence; review the market structure and your placement instead. Worked exercise and its limits An invented move from $100 to $98 and back to $101 may cross an assumed stop at $99. Compare an ordinary liquidity change and alleged manipulation as competing explanations. The price path alone cannot decide between them; no resting stop order is supported here. pages.title: Leverage Trading — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: Leverage is exposure greater than the supporting equity or collateral; losses can exceed the initial investment.
pages.content: Leverage Trading — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Leverage Trading — Trading Wiki Leverage is exposure greater than the supporting equity or collateral; losses can exceed the initial investment. At 10x leverage, $1,000 of margin controls roughly $10,000 of exposure. Leverage amplifies both gains and losses. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Leverage describes notional exposure relative to the equity or collateral supporting it. A hypothetical $1,000 margin amount supporting $10,000 exposure gives a 10-to-one ratio. A 10% adverse price move on that exposure is $1,000 before costs, but this is not a liquidation formula. Initial and maintenance requirements, eligible collateral, other positions, fees and venue rules all matter. A loan-funded share purchase differs from a futures performance bond or a perpetual contract. Product eligibility and maximum permitted exposure vary by jurisdiction, customer category, broker and instrument. An advertised maximum is neither permission for a particular user nor a recommendation. TradeHQ’s ordinary spot practice orders do not borrow money or reproduce a leveraged account. A worksheet can compare price shocks, account equity and cash-flow demands while keeping legal eligibility and actual margin terms as separate questions. Hypothetical worksheet: an account with $1,500 equity and $10,000 exposure loses $300 on a 3% adverse move before fees. Equity becomes $1,200. The initial exposure-to-account-equity ratio was about 6.67, even if only $1,000 had been labelled posted margin. This is why the denominator and eligible collateral must be stated; no exchange liquidation threshold is supplied by that arithmetic. Key points Greater exposure relative to equity magnifies linear gains and losses before costs; actual product outcomes can differ Liquidation depends on maintenance requirements and venue rules and can occur before the deposit is exhausted No universal professional leverage limit is established here Why it matters when you are learning Use a hypothetical exposure-to-equity calculation to compare gains and losses. TradeHQ does not implement leverage, and completing the exercise does not establish suitability for a real margin account. Worked exercise and its limits Compare unleveraged $1,000 exposure with $10,000 exposure supported by $1,000 collateral. A 2% adverse move means $20 versus $200 before costs. This linear illustration omits liquidation and funding; the TradeHQ order engine is unleveraged. pages.description: FOMO is the anxiety-driven urge to trade because a price is moving or others appear to be profiting.
pages.content: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) — Trading Wiki Learning notes: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) — Trading Wiki FOMO is the anxiety-driven urge to trade because a price is moving or others appear to be profiting. The emotion does not identify a market top or establish a measured win rate. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth FOMO means fear of missing out. In market discussions it can describe concern about missing apparent gains or pressure to imitate a publicly shared trade. The label does not diagnose a condition, identify someone’s motives from their purchase or measure future returns. Selectively published gains omit unknown losses, costs and unsuccessful participants. A learner can record what was known before a simulated decision and what was learned later, keeping the price outcome separate from the quality of the reasoning. No neurological claim, universal loss rate or promise that journaling improves returns is established here. Key points Emotional response to seeing rapid price increases Emotion alone does not establish where a market top is or a measured loss probability A written record separates the available information from later outcomes; it does not establish emotional or investment benefits Why it matters when you are learning Compare the recorded reason for a virtual decision with the information available at that time. The exercise does not diagnose a person or distinguish professionals from amateurs. Worked exercise and its limits Write down what information was available before an imagined purchase and what was learned later. Separate a rising price from a claim that everyone else profited. This record cannot diagnose a person or establish the effect of an emotion on future prices. pages.title: FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: FUD means fear, uncertainty and doubt.
pages.content: FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) — Trading Wiki Learning notes: FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) — Trading Wiki FUD means fear, uncertainty and doubt. The label is often applied to negative claims; it does not establish whether a claim is true, false or deliberately manipulative. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth FUD means fear, uncertainty and doubt. It is often applied to negative claims about a company, token or market. Calling a claim FUD does not establish whether it is accurate, mistaken or intentionally deceptive. Identify the original source, publication date, evidence and exact allegation; distinguish a regulatory announcement from commentary about its likely price effects. A later price rise does not disprove an earlier risk, and a decline does not verify every allegation. The exercise concerns information checking rather than diagnosing emotions, inferring a short seller’s motives or forecasting a market response. Key points Can be legitimate concerns or deliberate manipulation Negative claims can spread on social media; check their source and evidence Always verify FUD claims through official sources before reacting Why it matters when you are learning Check a negative claim’s original source and date. A concern can be material, mistaken or uncertain; a prior thesis does not turn every adverse report into a buying opportunity. Worked exercise and its limits Take a fictional alarming headline and separate its factual claim, original source, publication date and interpretation. Explain why labelling it FUD neither disproves the claim nor establishes the author's motive. pages.title: HODL Strategy — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: HODL is a buy-and-hold expression associated with a Bitcoin forum typo.
pages.content: HODL Strategy — Trading Wiki Learning notes: HODL Strategy — Trading Wiki HODL is a buy-and-hold expression associated with a Bitcoin forum typo. Holding through volatility can still produce losses; neither a four-year period nor an earlier price history guarantees recovery. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth HODL is informal language for retaining a crypto holding through price fluctuations. It is not a contractual protection, a guaranteed recovery rule or a distinct instrument. A single purchase and a recurring contribution schedule are different cash flows, and either can be held for a long period. A token can lose most or all of its value, become difficult to sell or be lost through custody failure. A published issuance rule alone cannot establish demand, purchasing power or future price. The linked Bitcoin white paper explains the protocol proposal; it does not validate a profitable holding strategy. Key points Originated from a 2013 Bitcoin forum typo ('HODL' instead of 'HOLD') Fewer transactions may reduce trading costs while price and timing risks remain A holding period does not protect against permanent loss, custody failure or illiquidity Why it matters when you are learning Compare a hypothetical holding period with an exit case, including permanent loss. Holding longer does not remove emotional decisions or guarantee a recovery. Worked exercise and its limits For an invented $1,000 holding, compare end values of $1,400, $600 and zero after the same period. Holding without selling does not remove market loss or custody risk. The white paper is protocol background, not evidence for a profitable holding strategy. Identity and ownership of wallets attributed to the creator remain uncertain. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach .
