This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Satoshi Nakamoto is the name attached to the Bitcoin white paper, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System. The document proposes electronic payments using cryptographic proof and a distributed timestamp mechanism. The name does not establish a verified individual identity. Claims about personal wealth, motives or ownership of particular early-mined coins require evidence beyond the paper and are not established here. Reading the original proposal helps separate its protocol design from later commentary about Bitcoin’s investment value. Neither the author’s identity nor a protocol description supplies a forecast of token prices. Key points Published the Bitcoin whitepaper on October 31, 2008 Wallet attribution and estimated holdings are uncertain; no exact ownership total is asserted here True identity remains unknown — one of tech's biggest mysteries Why it matters when you are learning Bitcoin's 2008 proposal drew on earlier cryptographic research. Reading the dated announcement and its references helps distinguish the documented protocol from later claims about the author's identity and holdings. Worked exercise and its limits Read the white paper's title, author name and timestamp proposal. Separate statements in the document from later claims about the author's identity or holdings. A pseudonym and address analysis do not establish a verified real-world identity. pages.title: Margin Call — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: A demand for additional collateral under an account’s margin terms.
pages.content: Margin Call — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Margin Call — Trading Wiki A demand for additional collateral under an account’s margin terms. A broker may reduce or liquidate positions under its rules; a call does not guarantee a response period. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth A margin call concerns collateral under a particular account agreement. In a loan-funded securities account, equity is the marked asset value less the loan and relevant obligations. Initial and maintenance requirements differ, and a broker can impose house requirements or change them. Futures performance-bond arrangements are a different mechanism from borrowing to purchase shares. Do not transfer a percentage or deadline between products. The linked SEC bulletin warns that a brokerage may sell securities without consulting the customer and that an extension is not an entitlement. Depositing collateral, reducing exposure or liquidation can change the account, but none guarantees a chosen exit price or caps every loss. TradeHQ has no margin accounts. Use the hypothetical equity calculation below to study the denominator, then keep actual broker procedures as a separate source-reading question. Key points Collateral obligations depend on the account agreement and maintenance rules; forced closing can occur without a prior call A broker may reduce or liquidate positions under its agreement; no guaranteed warning or response window is implied Multiple simultaneous margin calls can amplify market crashes Why it matters when you are learning Read the relevant maintenance and liquidation terms. A margin call can require action quickly, and no lesson or alert guarantees time to respond. TradeHQ has no margin accounts. Worked exercise and its limits Hypothetical account: $10,000 securities minus a $6,000 loan leave $4,000 equity. If securities fall to $8,000 with the loan unchanged, equity is $2,000, or 25% of asset value. Compare a stated maintenance requirement; do not invent the broker's call or liquidation procedure. pages.title: Liquidation Price — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: A liquidation price is an estimate of the level at which a leveraged position may be closed under a platform's margin rules.
pages.content: Liquidation Price — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Liquidation Price — Trading Wiki A liquidation price is an estimate of the level at which a leveraged position may be closed under a platform's margin rules. Collateral, fees, other positions and the pricing method can change that estimate. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth A liquidation price is a venue-calculated threshold used in managing a collateralized position. It is not necessarily an executable price or the price that consumes every dollar of equity. Maintenance requirements, other positions, eligible collateral, fees, funding and mark-price rules affect the threshold. Actual closing orders may execute differently during a gap or liquidity shortage. Isolated and cross-margin arrangements allocate eligible collateral differently; neither label establishes a universal cap on losses or account obligations. Consult a specific contract and venue rules for an actual calculation. TradeHQ’s unleveraged spot simulation has no liquidation-price engine. Key points With other inputs fixed, greater exposure leaves less collateral buffer; an exact threshold depends on the applicable rules Isolated-margin treatment depends on the platform rules; it is not a universal loss guarantee Mark price vs last price affects when liquidation triggers Why it matters when you are learning Compare the inputs in a venue’s documented estimate rather than treating one displayed price as fixed. Margin requirements and other positions can change the result. Worked exercise and its limits Distinguish a simplified collateral-loss calculation from an actual venue liquidation price. Fees, maintenance tiers, mark prices and collateral mode affect the latter. No single entry-price/leverage formula establishes a universal guaranteed exit, and TradeHQ does not model liquidation. pages.title: Dollar Cost Averaging — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: Dollar-cost averaging means contributing fixed amounts at regular intervals regardless of price.
pages.content: Dollar Cost Averaging — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Dollar Cost Averaging — Trading Wiki Dollar-cost averaging means contributing fixed amounts at regular intervals regardless of price. It changes purchase timing and the units acquired; it does not guarantee a lower average cost or outperform a lump-sum investment. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Dollar Cost Averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy where a fixed dollar amount is invested into a specific asset at regular intervals — weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly — regardless of the asset's current price. Equal contributions buy more units at lower prices and fewer at higher prices. The resulting average cost can be above or below a lump-sum purchase; the price sequence and costs determine the comparison. Price variation changes the units acquired under a fixed contribution schedule; that is a purchase-timing effect rather than a guaranteed mathematical advantage. In a volatile asset like Bitcoin, a $500 monthly investment over 12 months will purchase more BTC during months when the price is depressed and less during price peaks. A fixed schedule reduces decisions about purchase dates but does not eliminate emotion, automate every product or guarantee a better result. For a hypothetical example without fees, investing $100 when a unit costs $10 buys 10 units; another $100 at $20 buys 5. The combined 15 units cost $200, or about $13.33 per unit. Investing the same $200 entirely at the first $10 price would buy 20 units, while investing it entirely at $20 would buy 10. These examples show how timing changes the quantity purchased. They do not imply that either contribution schedule will outperform across a different price path or after costs. Key points Fixed amount invested at regular intervals regardless of price Equal scheduled contributions buy more units at lower prices and fewer at higher prices; DCA is distinct from a discretionary decision to add to a losing position A schedule defines purchase timing without eliminating emotion or guaranteeing a better result Why it matters when you are learning Calculate units bought under equal contributions at different hypothetical prices. Compare the same total cash over the same dates; a schedule does not establish a better return. Worked exercise and its limits With fee-free $100 contributions at $10 and $5, buy 10 + 20 = 30 units for $200. Average purchase cost is about $6.67, yet at $5 the holding is worth $150, a $50 loss. A lower average cost does not imply a gain. pages.title: Swing Trading — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: Holding positions across sessions, commonly for days or weeks.
pages.content: Swing Trading — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Swing Trading — Trading Wiki Holding positions across sessions, commonly for days or weeks. Review schedules and chart intervals vary; gaps and execution risks remain. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Swing trading describes a holding-period style in which positions commonly remain open across multiple sessions. It is not a standardized contract or proof that a particular schedule suits someone with a job or school commitments. Prices can gap during closed sessions, and an intended exit can execute at a different price or fail during a halt or outage. Chart intervals and review schedules are choices rather than universal professional standards. Compare holding windows using matching dates, costs and assumptions, keeping missed reviews and adverse cases in the record. TradeHQ’s instant practice fills omit real order-book execution. Key points Holds positions days to weeks to capture medium-term moves Chart intervals are choices for the stated exercise rather than a universal requirement Time requirements vary with the process and instruments; no universal daily schedule is established Why it matters when you are learning Compare a multi-day holding window with a shorter one, including gaps between observations. No holding period is a universal best starting method for beginners. Worked exercise and its limits A hypothetical share bought at $50 with an intended manual exit at $48 opens at $45 next session. For 20 shares, loss at $45 is $100 before costs, not the intended $40. Holding across sessions leaves gap and execution exposure. pages.description: Day trading means opening and closing positions within a trading day.
pages.content: Day Trading — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Day Trading — Trading Wiki Day trading means opening and closing positions within a trading day. It reduces exposure to overnight moves while retaining intraday price, execution and cost risks; no universal loss rate is asserted. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Day trading describes opening and closing positions within the same trading day. Fully closing a position removes that position’s later price exposure, but an intended close can be interrupted by a halt, outage or liquidity shortage. Frequent transactions can make spread, commission and slippage important even when gross gains look positive. Neither full-time screen use nor a fixed number of transactions establishes competence or profitability. Margin and account requirements depend on current venue, broker and jurisdiction rules. This entry does not assert a universal retail loss rate. TradeHQ is a virtual spot simulator, not a brokerage or a margin account. Key points All positions opened and closed within the same trading day Regulator education warns that intraday trading can cause substantial losses in a short period; no universal loss rate is asserted Real account margin and day-trading requirements depend on current rules, broker and jurisdiction Why it matters when you are learning Compare the time demands and assumptions of swing and intraday examples; practice profit alone does not establish readiness for real-money trading. Worked exercise and its limits A hypothetical 100-share purchase at $20 and sale at $20.10 gains $10 gross. If total modeled costs are $12, the net result is a $2 loss. Closing the position removes its later price exposure, but does not establish that repeated intraday trading is profitable. pages.title: Scalping — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: Scalping describes attempts to capture small price movements over short holding periods.
pages.content: Scalping — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Scalping — Trading Wiki Scalping describes attempts to capture small price movements over short holding periods. Execution and costs can outweigh gross gains. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Scalping is a short-holding-period style aimed at small price movements, often over seconds or minutes. A description of the objective is not evidence that the movements can be captured profitably. Latency, queue position, partial fills, spreads and commissions can matter relative to a small target. More transactions multiply costs as well as opportunities; the number alone cannot establish positive expectancy. Not every account offers the same execution or fee terms. TradeHQ’s displayed-price market fills do not reproduce an exchange order book, maker rebates or high-frequency infrastructure, so tiny simulated gains cannot validate an executable scalping strategy. Key points Attempts to profit from small movements over short periods; actual net results can be negative Short-horizon price targets can be overwhelmed by spread, fees, slippage and slow execution Break-even win rate depends on realized win and loss amounts plus costs Why it matters when you are learning Compare a small hypothetical gross price change with spreads, fees and worse fills. Discipline alone cannot remove execution risk or establish an investment edge. Worked exercise and its limits Ten invented round trips each gain $2 before $3 of round-trip costs: total net loss is $10. Vary costs before calling tiny gross moves profitable. TradeHQ fills do not reproduce queue priority, latency or an exchange order book. pages.title: Volume Profile — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: A volume profile groups recorded volume into price bins over a chosen interval.
pages.content: Volume Profile — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Volume Profile — Trading Wiki A volume profile groups recorded volume into price bins over a chosen interval. Its point of control is the highest-volume bin in that sample, not a forecast of where price must return. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth A volume profile groups observed trading volume into price bins over a stated sample. The point of control is the bin with the greatest volume under those settings. A value area encloses a selected share of volume using a specified construction method; a commonly chosen 70% share is not automatically one standard deviation or an economic valuation. Bin width, observation window and data coverage affect the result. A high-volume bin describes earlier activity and need not attract future price. TradeHQ does not supply a standard historical volume-profile overlay; a separate invented table is sufficient to learn the arithmetic. pages.description: Ichimoku Cloud displays several historical-price calculations with differing lookbacks and plotting offsets.
pages.content: Ichimoku Cloud — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Ichimoku Cloud — Trading Wiki Ichimoku Cloud displays several historical-price calculations with differing lookbacks and plotting offsets. Its Kumo cloud and other lines are chart conventions, not observations of future prices. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth The Ichimoku Cloud combines five historical-price calculations with different lookbacks and plotting offsets. The linked TradingView documentation describes its components and introduces its late-1960s publication history. A line plotted ahead of the latest candle still uses historical inputs; it does not observe future support or resistance. The five components are: Tenkan-sen (Conversion Line) — the midpoint of the highest high and lowest low over the past 9 periods, serving as a fast signal line. Kijun-sen (Base Line) — the midpoint over 26 periods, serving as a medium-term trend indicator and potential support/resistance. Senkou Span A (Leading Span A) — the average of Tenkan and Kijun lines, plotted 26 periods into the future. Senkou Span B (Leading Span B) — the midpoint of the highest high and lowest low over 52 periods, plotted 26 periods ahead. The shaded area between Senkou Span A and B forms the Cloud (Kumo) — the system's signature feature. Chikou Span (Lagging Span) — the current closing price plotted 26 periods in the past, used for confirmation. Trading signals in Ichimoku follow a hierarchy. One convention labels a bullish alignment when price is above the Cloud, Tenkan-sen is above Kijun-sen, Chikou Span is above the earlier price and Senkou Span A is above B. The alignment describes selected historical calculations; it is not a proven strongest signal. Key points Five historical-price calculations with different lookbacks and plotting offsets The cloud plots calculated historical values with a chosen displacement Component alignment describes related calculations without proving predictive strength Why it matters when you are learning Identify each lookback and plotting offset. A line displayed ahead of the current candle is calculated from historical prices, rather than knowledge of future support or resistance. Worked exercise and its limits On an external chart, record the lookback and plot displacement for each Ichimoku component. Moving a historical calculation forward on a chart does not make it future information. The cloud overlay is not supported by TradeHQ. In depth Elliott Wave Theory is an interpretive chart framework that labels selected movements as five-wave impulses and three-wave corrections. Additional conventions about overlap and relative wave lengths are used by its proponents, but different start points and intervals can produce competing counts. Labelling a price path after seeing it is prone to hindsight bias. For an educational exercise, draw two plausible counts on one invented series, state the criteria and extend the series to invalidate one of them. In depth A market maker quotes prices at which it is prepared to buy and sell under applicable venue rules. The ask-minus-bid difference is a quoted spread, not a guaranteed realized profit. Quotes can change; fills, inventory price changes, hedging and operating costs affect results. Obligations and permitted conduct differ between markets. A decentralized automated market maker is a different mechanism that applies a pool pricing rule rather than the same dealer quoting arrangement. Do not infer that a displayed quote will fill an arbitrary quantity or that a market maker always earns money. TradeHQ does not reproduce order queues or dealer inventory. Key points Quote bid and ask prices under venue rules; liquidity is not guaranteed for every order A quoted spread is not guaranteed net profit Automated market makers use protocol pricing rules and liquidity pools rather than conventional dealer quotes Why it matters when you are learning Compare quoted bid and ask prices with actual executions. Spread changes can have multiple explanations and do not establish a participant’s intent or sophistication. Worked exercise and its limits Hypothetical quotes: buy at $10 and sell at $10.02. Buying 100 units then selling them all at that ask earns $2 gross only if both executions occur. Inventory loss, hedging and costs can exceed that spread; a quote is not guaranteed profit. pages.description: Slippage is the difference between a stated reference price and an actual execution price.
pages.content: Slippage — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Slippage — Trading Wiki Slippage is the difference between a stated reference price and an actual execution price. It can be favorable or adverse; volatile conditions, limited liquidity and delays may increase it. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Slippage compares an actual execution price with a defined expected or reference price. The comparison requires a side, quantity and timestamp. Paying more than the reference on a purchase is adverse; paying less is favorable. A changing quote, limited available quantity or a delay can contribute to a difference, but a price series alone cannot isolate the cause. A limit price constrains eligible fills and may leave the order unfilled. It does not guarantee both execution and a particular outcome. TradeHQ's guest orders use a browser practice input; signed-in fills use a server-selected eligible quote, which can differ from the estimate. Neither models actual exchange liquidity. Key points Difference between expected and actual execution price Quote changes, liquidity constraints and delays can affect slippage even outside volatile periods Limit prices constrain eligible fills but do not ensure execution; market fills can differ from a quote Why it matters when you are learning Compare expected and weighted-average fill prices, with fees stated separately. A limit price can constrain execution but may leave the order unfilled; neither order type removes every risk. Worked exercise and its limits For an imagined 100-unit buy, a $10.05 fill versus an expected $10 costs $5 more. A $9.98 fill saves $2. Define the reference quote and timestamp; slippage can be favorable or adverse and differs from a separately charged commission. pages.title: Impermanent Loss — Explanation & Learning Exercise | TradeHQ Wiki
pages.description: Impermanent loss compares the value of a liquidity-provider position with simply holding the original tokens.
pages.content: Impermanent Loss — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Impermanent Loss — Trading Wiki Impermanent loss compares the value of a liquidity-provider position with simply holding the original tokens. The difference depends on the pool design and relative prices; fees and incentives also matter. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth For a fee-free, full-range constant-product pool initially balanced by value, compare the liquidity-provider position with holding the originally deposited assets. If their relative price changes by a factor r and arbitrage rebalances the pool, the relative value difference is 2×sqrt(r)/(1+r)−1 under these assumptions. At r=2 this is about −5.72%; at r=5 it is about −25.46%. This difference is a comparison with holding, not necessarily an absolute cash loss. Fees, incentives, concentrated ranges and token behavior change outcomes. Withdrawing does not create the earlier economic difference; a later price change can narrow or widen it. Smart-contract and custody risks are additional. Key points Value difference between LP position and simply holding the tokens In a simple fee-free constant-product pool, the relative value difference grows as paired-token prices diverge The value difference exists before withdrawal and can change with subsequent prices Why it matters when you are learning Compare liquidity provision with holding the same initial assets under a stated pool model. Fees, incentives and price changes all matter, alongside contract and withdrawal risks. Worked exercise and its limits For a fee-free full-range constant-product pool initially holding 1 token worth $100 and $100 cash, double the token price. Arbitrage gives about 0.7071 tokens and $141.42 cash, total $282.84 versus $300 holding: about 5.72% less. Fees, incentives and concentrated liquidity change the comparison. pages.description: US circuit breakers pause trading at specified thresholds. Learn how market-wide halts differ from individual-security pauses and why exits remain uncertain.
pages.content: Circuit Breaker — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Circuit Breaker — Trading Wiki A rule-defined trading pause. US market-wide thresholds use S&P 500 declines of 7%, 13% and 20%, with time-of-day conditions; individual-security and other-market rules differ. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Circuit breakers are rule-defined trading pauses. In the US market-wide example described by NYSE, declines from the previous S&P 500 close trigger three levels: 7%, 13% and 20%. In a regular session, a Level 1 or Level 2 event before 3:25 p.m. Eastern leads to a fifteen-minute halt; those levels at or after that time do not halt trading. Level 3 ends trading for the day. Check the current exchange rules and special-session arrangements rather than applying this example to every venue. Individual-security Limit Up-Limit Down rules are separate from a market-wide halt: price bands and pauses depend on the applicable plan. Neither mechanism guarantees an exit price or prevents losses, and a reopening can occur at a different price. Other markets and asset types can have different controls. For a hypothetical comparison, distinguish a 7% S&P 500 decline early in a regular session from the same decline after 3:25 p.m., then compare a Level 3 event. These are rule-reading exercises; TradeHQ does not execute exchange orders or reproduce every halt and reopening condition. Key points US market-wide halts at S&P 500 declines of 7%, 13%, and 20% Individual stock halts (LULD) prevent trades outside price bands Venue-specific crypto trading controls vary; do not assume US equity halt rules apply Why it matters when you are learning Read the current venue rules and distinguish a market-wide halt from an individual-security pause. A halt does not prevent every loss or establish a post-reopening opportunity. Worked exercise and its limits With a hypothetical prior S&P 500 close of 5,000, declines of 7%, 13% and 20% correspond to 4,650, 4,350 and 4,000. Apply the official time-of-day rules before predicting a halt; individual-security pauses use different rules. pages.description: A fraud scheme in which promoters use false or misleading claims to inflate an asset's price and sell their holdings at inflated prices, exposing later buyers to losses.
pages.content: Pump and Dump — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Pump and Dump — Trading Wiki A fraud scheme in which promoters use false or misleading claims to inflate an asset's price and sell their holdings at inflated prices, exposing later buyers to losses. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Pump-and-dump schemes use false or misleading promotion to stimulate buying and inflate a price while promoters seek to sell their own holdings. The SEC's linked explanation describes this mechanism for stocks; the CFTC also warns about virtual-currency pump-and-dump schemes. A scheme does not require a predictable five-stage timeline or a sale at the exact price peak. Promotion and selling can overlap, and a price chart alone cannot establish who sold or whether a statement was fraudulent. Thin liquidity can make exits difficult, but an abrupt rise or fall is not itself proof of manipulation. Check the original claim, its date, the promoter's disclosed interests and the relevant issuer or project disclosures. A coordinated countdown, unsupported promise or undisclosed incentive warrants investigation rather than a guaranteed detection rule. Keep the evidence for a misleading statement separate from a hypothetical price scenario. This lesson explains a fraud mechanism; it does not determine whether a particular token, issuer or person violated a law. Key points False or misleading promotion can inflate a price while promoters seek to sell their holdings A fixed timeline, exact peak sale or price move alone does not establish the scheme Check claims, disclosures and promoter incentives against primary evidence Why it matters when you are learning Check claims against primary disclosures and consider incentives behind a promotion. A social-media mention alone does not prove fraud, while coordinated misleading promotion warrants caution. Worked exercise and its limits For a fictional promotion, list the promoter's disclosed interest, independently verifiable evidence and promised outcome. Paid hype and a price rise are warning context, while establishing an offence requires evidence and applicable law. Do not treat a suspicious message as a price signal. pages.description: The risk-reward ratio compares a trade's planned loss with its planned gain.
pages.content: Risk-Reward Ratio — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Risk-Reward Ratio — Trading Wiki The risk-reward ratio compares a trade's planned loss with its planned gain. A 1:3 ratio means a planned $1 loss for a potential $3 gain; it does not guarantee those fills or establish a universal professional minimum. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth The risk-reward ratio (R:R or RRR) is a measurement that compares the potential loss on a trade (from entry to stop loss) against the potential gain (from entry to take profit target). Expressed as a ratio like 1:2 or 1:3, it quantifies the trade's payoff structure before entry, describing a hypothetical payoff structure, not determining whether a real transaction is suitable. A 1:2 risk-reward ratio means that for every dollar risked, two dollars of profit are targeted. A 1:3 ratio means three dollars of potential profit for each dollar of risk. A planned ratio describes selected entry and exit assumptions. A break-even calculation requires realised payoff sizes and costs; the planned ratio alone does not determine profitability. For fixed realised payoffs before costs, a 1:1 ratio breaks even at 50% wins; profitability requires more than 50%. Planned exits do not ensure those realised payoffs. With fixed realized +2R/−1R before costs, the exact break-even rate is one third; profitability requires a higher rate. At 1:3 with fixed realised gains and losses, a win rate above 25% is required before costs; exactly 25% breaks even. Under stated fixed-payoff assumptions, expected value combines the frequency and size of gains and losses. Costs and dependence also matter, and an estimate from one historical sample does not establish a future positive expectancy. A chosen planned payoff ratio is not a universal fund rule or evidence of positive realised expectancy. Use the same monetary units for the two assumed outcomes and state the convention. A hypothetical $5 loss and $15 gain give risk:reward of 1:3; gain divided by loss is instead the reward-to-risk multiple of 3. Neither describes an assured outcome. Key points Compares potential loss (stop loss) to potential gain (take profit) With fixed realized +3R/−1R before costs, 25% wins breaks even; profitability requires more A planned ratio is not a universal professional minimum or evidence of positive expectancy Why it matters when you are learning Calculate the planned ratio, then compare it with realised gains, losses and costs. A favorable planned ratio is not proof that the outcomes will match it. Worked exercise and its limits With fixed realized wins of +$3 and losses of −$1, a 25% win rate gives 0.25×3 − 0.75×1 = zero before costs. Adding any positive cost makes that result negative. Planned stops and targets do not establish realized amounts or win probabilities. pages.content: Drawdown — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Drawdown — Trading Wiki Drawdown measures a decline from a previously observed peak to a later lower value, including an unfinished decline. Maximum drawdown is the largest such decline in a specified sample, not a ceiling on future loss. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Drawdown measures a decline from an observed peak to a later lower value within a defined series. Maximum drawdown is the largest such peak-to-trough decline in the chosen sample, not the worst loss that could occur in the future. State whether observations include fees, cash flows and mark-to-market positions; an end-of-day sample can miss an intraday trough. A drop from $100 to $80 is 20%, but recovering from $80 to $100 requires 25%. Deposits can make raw portfolio-value comparisons misleading. The arithmetic does not diagnose stress or predict whether someone would tolerate a real loss. Key points Observed peak-to-trough decline under the specified valuation and sampling method 50% drawdown requires 100% gain to recover — math is asymmetric Sampling frequency and cash-flow treatment can affect a measured drawdown; state the method before comparing results Why it matters when you are learning Calculate the decline from the relevant peak and state the observation period. Historical maximum drawdown is not an upper bound on future loss, and no universal percentage is a suitable limit for everyone. Worked exercise and its limits An invented portfolio peaks at $100,000 and falls to $80,000: drawdown is 20%. Returning to the peak needs $20,000/$80,000 = 25% growth. Deposits can distort a raw-value comparison; this example assumes none. pages.description: Backtesting applies stated rules to historical data to examine hypothetical results.
pages.content: Backtesting — Trading Wiki Learning notes: Backtesting — Trading Wiki Backtesting applies stated rules to historical data to examine hypothetical results. It can reveal problems with an idea but does not validate future performance; look-ahead, survivorship and overfitting bias matter. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth Backtesting applies predefined rules to historical observations under stated execution and accounting assumptions. Its results describe that selected dataset; they are not executed returns or proof of a future advantage. Look-ahead bias uses information unavailable at the decision time, survivorship bias omits failed or unavailable instruments, and repeated parameter searches can overfit the same history. Separate rule development from held-out evaluation, document the searches performed and account for costs and missing observations. There is no universal number of years or trades that validates a strategy. Generated simulator candles are not historical market observations. Key points Simulates strategy performance using historical price data Overfitting can make selected historical results misleading Out-of-sample testing can challenge overfitting but cannot establish a guaranteed future edge Why it matters when you are learning Keep rule development separate from evaluation on unseen historical data. Record costs and failed cases. Neither backtesting nor forward simulation certifies future investment performance. Worked exercise and its limits Write a rule using a development sample, then freeze it before examining a held-out sample. Include costs, missing data and delisted instruments where relevant. A generated simulator chart is not historical market evidence, and a held-out gain does not guarantee future performance. pages.content: What Is Paper Trading? Practice, Uses and Limitations Learning notes: What Is Paper Trading? Practice, Uses and Limitations Paper trading uses virtual money to explore order placement, portfolio arithmetic and record-keeping. It avoids real-money trades, but cannot reproduce all live-market costs or risks. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . This does not verify every learning claim or constitute independent professional review. What Is Paper Trading? Paper trading is the practice of simulating trades without using real money. Instead of risking your hard-earned savings, you use virtual currency to buy and sell stocks, ETFs, cryptocurrencies, and other financial instruments. The name refers to recording hypothetical transactions rather than sending real orders. Today, paper trading is usually done digitally through simulated platforms. It can help beginners practise order entry, chart reading, record-keeping, and portfolio mechanics without risking real money. It is one practical way to learn how markets work, but it cannot reproduce every part of live trading, especially slippage, liquidity constraints, and the emotions attached to real losses. TradeHQ starts new practice portfolios with $100,000 in virtual cash. Its catalogue contains 170 instrument examples, including legacy entries; not every entry represents a currently available real-market instrument. Practice orders and resulting positions appear in the simulator's records, subject to its stated guest and account-data limitations. This is not a brokerage execution record. What Beginners Can Practise Paper trading gives you a controlled environment to make mistakes, test a process, and learn the mechanics before real money is involved. There is no universal number of practice weeks or months that guarantees better results. A more useful goal is to practise until you can follow the same written process consistently across a meaningful sample of simulated trades. A virtual exercise can compare day trading, swing trading and buy-and-hold under the same stated assumptions. Record hypothetical entries and exits and review gains and losses over a meaningful sample. TradeHQ executes market orders; stop and limit orders are explained conceptually rather than implemented as pending orders. Paper trading can also be used to practise risk management. You can test position sizing, predefined exit rules, diversification, and the discipline of writing a trading plan before placing an order. Any percentage risk limit should be treated as a practice parameter, not a universal rule. How to Get Started with Paper Trading on TradeHQ Visit TradeHQ to start with $100,000 in virtual cash. Browse the asset catalogue, read the practice-data labels, place a simulated market order, and review the portfolio accounting. The practice snapshot is descriptive and need not reflect actual news or market execution. The mentor offers rule-based educational prompts about a practice portfolio. Use those prompts as questions for a journal, rather than personalized investment recommendations. Compare what was expected with what happened in the simulation and record where an assumption failed. A simulator can help document a process before testing it elsewhere, but virtual results do not establish readiness for real-money trading. Liquidity, transaction costs, gaps, taxes and behaviour under real losses can differ. Learning the mechanics is the purpose of this exercise. pages.content: How to Read a Stock Chart: A Beginner's Guide Learning notes: How to Read a Stock Chart: A Beginner's Guide Learn to describe candlesticks, historical price movements and common indicator calculations without assuming that a recognizable pattern predicts returns. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. A limited source check dated 2026-10-31 is documented below, with its precise scope. This is not a full independent editorial or professional review; no independent professional review is claimed. Source-check scope Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: OHLC candlestick descriptions and standard indicator terminology were compared with the linked chart-learning materials. Pattern forecasts and trading outcomes have not been independently validated. Understanding the Basics of Stock Charts A stock chart is a visual representation of a security's price movement over time. The x-axis shows time (minutes, hours, days, or years) and the y-axis shows price. The most common chart types are line charts, bar charts, and candlestick charts. Candlesticks display four key observations: opening, high, low and closing prices. Each candlestick represents a specific time period. Many chart themes use green for a close above the open and red for a close below it. Colours and hollow-candle conventions vary; use the chart legend and the actual open and close values. The body of the candle shows the open-to-close range, while the thin lines above and below (called wicks or shadows) show the high and low. Candlestick names such as Doji, Hammer and Engulfing describe shapes in an observed price series. They do not prove that a reversal or continuation will occur. On TradeHQ, inspect whether the chart uses provider candles or generated practice candles before interpreting the displayed shape. Support, Resistance, and Trend Lines Support and resistance describe areas where a price has previously paused or changed direction. They are approximate chart observations rather than floors or ceilings. A price may cross a marked level and keep moving, so compare both continuation and reversal scenarios in a journal. Trend lines connect selected price points, such as higher lows or lower highs. Their placement depends on the observation period and chosen points. A break changes that chart description; it does not establish that a new trend will continue. Volume counts shares, contracts or units traded during a stated period. A price move with high volume is an observation to investigate, not proof of reliability or institutional intent. Compare the source, interval and alternative explanations before making a simulated assumption. Key Technical Indicators for Beginners Moving averages smooth a specified historical price series. A 50-period average crossing above a 200-period average is commonly called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. These lagging descriptions can change repeatedly and do not guarantee useful entry or exit timing. The Relative Strength Index (RSI) measures momentum on a scale of 0 to 100. Under common RSI settings, values above 70 are often labelled overbought and below 30 oversold. Those conventional labels are descriptions, not evidence that a reversal is imminent or certain. MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) is another momentum indicator that shows the relationship between two moving averages. Practice reading charts on TradeHQ by opening any asset page — for example, NVIDIA (NVDA) or Ethereum (ETH). Identify the chosen candle shapes and levels, recording the source, time interval and calculation settings. Compare cases where a labelled pattern is followed by continuation as well as reversal; observations on generated practice charts cannot validate historical predictive accuracy. pages.content: Crypto vs Stocks: Which Should You Practice Trading First? Learning notes: Crypto vs Stocks: Which Should You Practice Trading First? Crypto and stocks differ in market structure, trading hours and price risk. Compare the same virtual exposure and observation window rather than assuming either is the right starting point. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. A limited source check dated 2026-10-31 is documented below, with its precise scope. This is not a full independent editorial or professional review; no independent professional review is claimed. Source-check scope Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: listed-share versus crypto-asset exposure and variable regulatory protections were compared with SEC Investor.gov crypto-asset guidance. Market hours and issuer claims are descriptive, not investment recommendations. The Key Differences Between Crypto and Stocks A listed company share represents an ownership interest rather than direct ownership of the issuer's underlying assets. U.S.-listed public companies such as Apple publish financial disclosures under applicable securities rules; some companies pay dividends, but payouts are not guaranteed. The NYSE core equity session normally runs on trading weekdays from 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM Eastern Time; holidays, shortened sessions and other trading sessions are separate. Cryptocurrency networks differ in governance, issuance and degree of decentralization. Many crypto trading venues operate around the clock, although maintenance, outages and provider restrictions can interrupt access. Prices can move outside stock-exchange sessions, including weekends and holidays; continuous market hours do not guarantee that a particular venue or order is available. Price variability depends on the asset, observation period and market conditions. A cryptocurrency and a company share can both have large gains or losses; a typical daily percentage is not a fixed risk classification. Compare percentage changes over the same sample rather than assume a permanent volatility ranking. Company Disclosures and Market Rules Company reports provide information about revenue, expenses and business risks. Such information can inform an analysis without making a stock stable or its future return predictable. Any historical index return depends on the dates, reinvestment assumptions, inflation and costs used. Listed shares and cryptocurrencies can be subject to different disclosure, custody and market rules. These vary by jurisdiction and asset; regulation does not eliminate loss risk. Use dated company filings rather than assumptions about familiar brands when researching a historical price change. TradeHQ lets you study company examples using virtual cash. Treat a news explanation as a hypothesis and compare alternative outcomes. Generated simulator changes do not reproduce an earnings announcement or establish how the actual stock responded. What a Crypto Practice Example Teaches Differently Many cryptocurrency trading venues operate throughout weekends, but availability can be interrupted by outages, maintenance or restrictions. Observed price movements can be rapid or slow depending on the asset and period, and continuous access does not make learning easier or safer. An asset's unit price also does not measure its risk or accessibility; position size and total exposure matter more than whether one token costs less than $1. The crypto ecosystem introduces you to concepts like blockchain technology, decentralized finance (DeFi), and tokenomics — knowledge that helps you distinguish a network's function from a token's market price. Understanding both worlds can help you ask more precise questions about the risks. A learning exercise can compare one company example with one cryptocurrency using the same hypothetical position value and observation period. Record differences in mechanics and uncertainty without treating either market as the required starting choice. Virtual results do not establish real-money suitability. Buy and Hold (A Holding-Period Hypothesis) Buy and hold means retaining an investment over a longer period instead of trading each short-term move. A business can lose value permanently, and patience does not guarantee recovery. In a simulation, define the observation period and compare a hold with alternative rules under the same assumptions. A virtual holding can be marked at several assumed later prices to compare a hold with a different hypothetical rule. Results depend on the window, costs, source quotes and omitted distributions. A lower price might be a lasting loss rather than a temporary dip. For an educational company comparison, record revenue, costs, debt and business assumptions before observing later results. The mentor provides rule-based practice prompts, not a forecast or a recommendation to commit capital. Distinguish information available at the time from hindsight. 2. Swing Trading (Capturing Multi-Day Moves) Swing trading involves holding positions for several days to weeks, aiming to capture medium-term price moves. Holding overnight introduces gaps and news exposure. A written example can compare review schedules, but a holding period does not establish suitability for a particular person or guarantee that less monitoring is sufficient. A swing-trading hypothesis may refer to support, resistance or a chosen chart pattern. Those descriptions do not identify an asset that is certainly about to move. Record an entry assumption and hypothetical exit, then compare alternative outcomes and the effect of gaps or costs. Compare virtual swing-trading examples with a simple hold over the same period. Record entry, exit and sample size in a journal. TradeHQ implements market orders; a stop or target recorded in the journal does not automatically execute. A short sample cannot establish a dependable edge. 3. Momentum Trading, 4. Mean Reversion, and 5. Dollar-Cost Averaging Momentum methods use past price changes to define a rule for studying continuation. A trend may reverse after entry. Compare a precisely specified hypothetical rule with a simple baseline rather than treat a moving average or RSI reading as confirmation of the next move. Mean-reversion methods test whether deviations from a specified average tend to narrow in a chosen sample. A price may remain far from its average or continue moving away. Define the sample, exit assumption and costs before interpreting any simulated result. Dollar-cost averaging means contributing a fixed amount at regular intervals. It changes purchase timing and units acquired, but it does not guarantee a lower average cost or remove loss risk. Compare scheduled hypothetical purchases with a lump-sum example using the same total contribution and dates. Compare the five methods as educational hypotheses with a common starting balance, period and cost assumptions. Record failed assumptions as carefully as favourable outcomes. Neither a comfortable routine nor several successful practice weeks proves that a method will work with real money. pages.content: What Is a Stock Market Index and How Do ETFs Work? Learning notes: What Is a Stock Market Index and How Do ETFs Work? Compare different stock-index methodologies and learn how index-tracking ETFs provide specified exposure rather than ownership of an entire market. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. A limited source check dated 2026-10-31 is documented below, with its precise scope. This is not a full independent editorial or professional review; no independent professional review is claimed. Source-check scope Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: ETF ownership, fund-diversification limitations and the distinction between an index and a fund were compared with SEC Investor.gov fund guidance. Named index methodology and current holdings require dated issuer documents. What Is a Stock Market Index? A stock index summarizes a selected set of securities using published rules. The S&P 500 measures a large-company segment using float-adjusted market-capitalization weighting, the Nasdaq Composite covers eligible Nasdaq-listed common-type securities, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index of 30 companies. The Nasdaq-100 is a distinct index covering a selected group of large non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies. These have different constituents and weighting methods; consult dated index methodology documents for current details. An index is a calculation rather than a security purchased directly. Some exchange-traded funds seek to track named indexes using a specified portfolio and method. Fees, replication choices and distributions can cause a fund's return to differ from a reported index. When a report states that 'the market' rose, identify its index, interval, currency and dividend treatment. A price index, total-return index and tracking ETF are distinct observations. How ETFs Work An ETF has shares that trade on an exchange and pursues an objective specified in its prospectus. Examples include SPY (S&P 500), QQQ (Nasdaq-100) and DIA (Dow Jones Industrial Average). An ETF shareholder owns shares of that fund rather than separately registered shares in every underlying company. Holdings, fees and returns may differ from those of its reference index. An ETF provides the exposure specified by its objective and holdings. Diversification, concentration, leverage, annual expenses and trading costs vary by fund; low cost or broad diversification is not guaranteed. Read the current fund documents before interpreting a historical comparison. Compare ETF examples with an individual company using the same period and position value in the simulator. Examine holdings and concentration rather than treating any fund as a universally appropriate beginner investment. Several funds can hold overlapping securities. No asset allocation or rebalancing schedule is recommended. The Foundation: Asset Allocation Asset allocation divides a portfolio across selected asset classes or holdings. Its effect depends on exposures, correlations and the period examined. Allocation does not guarantee diversification or performance; document the assumptions rather than rank it as universally more important than every other decision. For a virtual accounting example, choose percentages that total 100%, such as 60% in a stock-index example, 30% cash and 10% another practice asset. These numbers illustrate weighting only. Compare another normalized allocation and identify overlapping holdings and concentration. Real-money allocation depends on circumstances including objectives, time horizon, liabilities and ability to bear loss. Age alone cannot determine a suitable stock/bond split. A simulator can compare hypothetical exposures, but it cannot discover a person's true risk tolerance or certify an investment allocation. Diversification: Don't Put All Eggs in One Basket Diversification distributes selected exposures but cannot prevent several holdings declining together. For arithmetic practice, if a sector is 25% of a $100,000 virtual portfolio and falls 30% while everything else stays unchanged, that sector contributes a $7,500 loss before costs. Actual results depend on overlapping holdings and how other prices change. Compare exposures by issuer, sector, geography, currency and economic sensitivity. More tickers do not necessarily mean less concentration when holdings overlap. An index fund provides a specified basket, not every type of protection. Compare a concentrated virtual portfolio with one spread across different practice exposures. Keep total starting value and observation period equal and record each contribution to gains and losses. A commodity or ETF is not an assured hedge; correlations and fund holdings can change. Rebalancing and Ongoing Management Portfolio weights can drift as holdings change in value. In a hypothetical portfolio with no cash flows, a 50% crypto gain and a 10% stock gain increase crypto's relative weight. This changes sensitivity to crypto; the calculation alone does not determine the portfolio's overall risk. Rebalancing adjusts toward selected target weights through purchases, sales or new contributions where available. Targets are study assumptions, and fees, taxes and subsequent price changes affect the comparison. Rebalancing does not guarantee smaller losses or higher returns. Rebalancing adjusts holdings toward selected target weights, subject to fills, rounding and costs. Timing and thresholds are choices to compare, not universal quarterly or five-percent rules. Rebalancing can add costs and can reduce returns in a continuing trend, so record turnover and compare against a portfolio left unchanged. For an educational rebalancing worksheet, set hypothetical weights, recalculate them after invented price changes and quantify the effect of virtual transaction fees. Compare the adjusted portfolio with one left unchanged. No allocation, monthly schedule or calculated benefit should be treated as a recommendation for a real account. pages.content: Risk Management for Paper Trading: Risk Budgets and Exits Learning notes: Risk Management for Paper Trading: Risk Budgets and Exits Study position sizing, conceptual exits and risk-budget arithmetic. TradeHQ supports manual market orders; percentage rules such as 1% or 2% are worksheet assumptions. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . Source-check scope Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited calculation and source check: 0.4×2−0.6×1=0.2, 0.25×3−0.75×1=0, and 192×(5+0.10+0.095)=997.44 were recalculated. SEC order guidance supports the limitations of stop orders. No strategy performance or suitability claim was verified. Measuring Risk Alongside Trade Outcomes Risk management describes how exposure and losses are measured or limited under a chosen process. Profitability also depends on realized gains, losses, frequency and costs. For example, a 40% win rate with fixed 2R gains and 1R losses has gross expectancy 0.4×2−0.6×1=0.2R per trade before costs; it is hypothetical arithmetic. Exposure rules and intended exits can be compared in a hypothetical worksheet, but they do not guarantee survival through a loss sequence or establish that a profitable edge exists. Gaps, costs and correlated holdings can create losses beyond a chosen assumption. On TradeHQ, you can practise risk-management ideas with $100,000 in virtual cash. Experiment with different position sizes, exit rules, and reward-to-risk assumptions, then review how each choice changes drawdown and variability over a larger sample of trades. The aim is to build a repeatable process, not to discover a guaranteed formula. Position Sizing With a Predefined Risk Limit Position sizing determines how much of your portfolio you expose to a single trade. Percentage-based limits such as 1% or 2% are common educational examples, but they are not universal prescriptions. On a $100,000 practice account, a 1% risk budget would be $1,000 and a 2% budget would be $2,000. For a hypothetical $100,000 account, a chosen 1% worksheet loss budget is $1,000. An entry at $100 and an assumed exit at $95 create a $5 price loss per share before costs. Dividing $1,000 by $5 gives 200 shares and a $20,000 entry notional, but that excludes fees. TradeHQ's 0.1% buy and sell fees add $20 at entry and $19 at that exit, making the total loss $1,039. To include those fees in the same assumed $1,000 budget, divide by $5 + $0.10 + $0.095 = $5.195 per share: rounding down to 192 whole shares gives a $997.44 loss at exactly $95. This remains a worksheet assumption, not a guaranteed maximum loss: a gap or different fill can exceed it, and TradeHQ does not execute an automatic stop. In a fixed-loss hypothetical model, smaller fractional losses reduce the cumulative decline relative to larger losses. Actual outcomes can exceed assumptions, particularly where fills, fees or simultaneous exposures differ. Use the simulator to compare several fixed-risk assumptions and record the resulting drawdowns rather than treating any single percentage as a magic number. Stop-Losses and Risk-Reward Ratios A stop order uses a trigger price, while its eventual fill depends on the order type and market conditions. Gaps or limited liquidity can produce a worse fill than the planned price. A journal exit assumption is useful for arithmetic but does not establish an exact maximum loss. Reward-to-risk compares an assumed gain with an assumed loss. With fixed realized 3R wins and 1R losses, a 25% win rate gives 0.25×3−0.75×1=0R gross expectancy before costs. A planned target need not be achieved, and fees can make even that break-even example negative. Compare position sizes and hypothetical exit rules in a practice journal, using the same observation period and stated cost assumptions. TradeHQ executes market orders and does not place automatic stop orders. Review drawdown, realized gains and losses, sample size and assumptions without treating any ratio as a guarantee. pages.title: Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Price Control and Execution Uncertainty | TradeHQ Learn

pages.content: Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Price Control and Execution Uncertainty Learning notes: Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Price Control and Execution Uncertainty Compare market and limit order mechanics, fill uncertainty and the situations each order type is designed for. TradeHQ only simulates market orders. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. A limited source check dated 2026-10-31 is documented below, with its precise scope. This is not a full independent editorial or professional review; no independent professional review is claimed. Source-check scope Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: market, limit and stop order definitions and execution/price uncertainty were compared with the SEC Investor.gov Types of Orders page. Hypothetical BTC prices are illustrative, not a verified market quotation. What Is a Market Order? A market order seeks execution at available prices rather than specifying a limit price. Execution and the final price depend on available liquidity, trading halts and other conditions. The displayed quote is not a guaranteed fill, particularly when prices move quickly. Market orders prioritize seeking execution over a specified price limit. That trade-off can involve substantial uncertainty in the eventual fill. Compare hypothetical outcomes under different liquidity and gap assumptions rather than prescribe one order type for every urgent situation. Slippage is the difference between an expected price and the actual fill. Its size varies with order size, liquidity and timing; it is not always pennies in a named asset. TradeHQ uses simplified practice market fills and does not reproduce every exchange execution condition. What Is a Limit Order? A limit order specifies the highest acceptable price for a buy or the lowest acceptable price for a sale; an execution may occur at a better price. A buy limit order executes only at your specified price or lower; a sell limit order executes only at your specified price or higher. Unlike market orders, limit orders give you price control but don't guarantee execution. In a hypothetical example, suppose Bitcoin is quoted at $68,000 while a buy limit is set at $65,000. If the market reaches that level, the order becomes eligible to fill, subject to available liquidity and order priority. A limit instruction can also be cancelled or expire before the quoted price reaches its boundary; its lifetime depends on the specified conditions. Limit orders can be useful when price control matters more than immediate execution. They are commonly used for planned entries and exits, but the trade-off is that the order may not fill at all, or may fill only partially, if there is not enough matching liquidity. When to Use Each Order Type A market order and a limit order make different trade-offs between seeking execution and controlling price. For a learning exercise, compare possible fills during a liquid session, a wide spread and a price gap. Neither urgency nor a familiar ticker guarantees a small execution cost. A limit order specifies a maximum buy price or minimum sell price. Price control does not guarantee any fill or a full fill, even when a chart touches the level. Compare an unfilled order with a partial fill and a completed fill in a written hypothetical example. TradeHQ currently executes market orders only. Study limit-order mechanics conceptually with a written example; there is no pending limit-order feature to test on SOL or another asset. Simulator fills cannot establish which order type gives better actual execution. pages.description: Understand RSI, MACD and moving-average calculations, how crossovers describe past prices, and why those observations cannot guarantee future returns.
pages.content: Technical Indicators Explained: RSI, MACD and Moving Averages Learning notes: Technical Indicators Explained: RSI, MACD and Moving Averages RSI, MACD and moving averages describe selected price observations. Learn their calculations, conventional interpretations and limits, then compare hypothetical examples without treating a signal as a trade recommendation. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. A limited source check dated 2026-10-18 is documented below, with its precise scope. This is not a full independent editorial or professional review; no independent professional review is claimed. Source-check scope Source check: 2026-10-18. RSI, MACD and moving-average definitions compared with the linked Fidelity guides; no predictive-performance or professional review claimed. Moving Averages: The Foundation of Trend Analysis Moving averages smooth a selected price series rather than establish a hidden or future trend. Two commonly used calculations are the simple moving average (SMA), which weights observations in its window equally, and the exponential moving average (EMA), which gives greater weight to recent observations. A 50-period average crossing above a 200-period average is called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. The period might mean days or another chart interval. These lagging observations describe the selected series and do not establish that a rally or decline will follow. Shorter averages such as a 9-period or 21-period EMA react differently from longer averages. A price above an average describes its position relative to that calculation, not a guaranteed trend. TradeHQ chart controls include moving-average and volume overlays; indicator examples should match the actual chart features. RSI: Measuring Momentum and Overbought/Oversold Conditions Standard RSI, introduced by J. Welles Wilder, expresses the relationship between smoothed gains and losses on a 0–100 scale. Fourteen periods is a common default; the conventional thresholds are descriptive labels rather than evidence of misvaluation or future direction. Readings above 70 or below 30 are conventional RSI descriptions rather than instructions to sell or buy. An extreme reading can persist. Divergence means price and oscillator observations differ; it does not prove a reversal or make one signal universally most reliable. Compare hypothetical RSI settings and record what each describes before looking at later prices. A pullback to 40–50 or a bounce to 50–60 is not a universal entry rule. TradeHQ's simplified RSI-style practice value should not be mistaken for a standard RSI calculation on historical provider closes. MACD: Combining Trend and Momentum Signals The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) is a versatile indicator that shows the relationship between two exponential moving averages — typically the 12-period and 26-period EMAs. The MACD line is the difference between these two EMAs, and the signal line is a 9-period EMA of the MACD line. The histogram shows the gap between them. A positive histogram means the MACD line is above its signal line; a negative histogram means it is below. Those relationships are often called bullish and bearish respectively, but describe the selected calculations rather than the next price move. Crossovers can reverse in both trending and sideways samples; performance depends on the rules, period, costs and comparison used. Combining indicators creates another hypothesis to evaluate, rather than guaranteeing the best results. Define each calculation, interval and decision rule, then compare against a simple baseline with the same costs and sample. TradeHQ does not provide a MACD chart overlay; journal examples are conceptual. pages.description: Bitcoin and Ethereum are digital networks with different transaction and application designs.
pages.content: Bitcoin vs Ethereum Learning notes: Bitcoin vs Ethereum Bitcoin and Ethereum are digital networks with different transaction and application designs. Compare their supply rules, uses and costs without treating either token as a savings plan or predicting its price. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. How the two differ in practice Bitcoin transactions transfer value under rules verified by network participants. Ethereum also supports applications through smart contracts. Those mechanisms raise different research questions: how transactions are validated, what users pay to transact, how protocol changes are adopted and how application execution works. Neither design guarantees demand for its token. Use the network documentation to distinguish technical rules from a claim about savings, purchasing power or future market price. For a practice comparison, measure BTC and ETH returns over the same observation period. Correlation depends on that sample and can change; two token names do not by themselves establish independent exposures. Record the market-data source, interval and method before interpreting a relationship. Network activity, fees and issuance are additional variables to investigate rather than guaranteed leading indicators. A BTC/ETH split changes weights but does not prove diversification or prescribe a suitable total crypto allocation. Key differences Supply: compare Bitcoin issuance rules with Ethereum issuance and fee burning; Ethereum supply changes with network conditions. Staking: Ethereum rewards, fees, withdrawal arrangements and risks vary; TradeHQ does not model staking returns. Use case: compare settlement and programmability using each network’s current documentation. Volatility: compare percentage changes over the same stated sample rather than use a fixed ETH/BTC volatility multiple. What the comparison shows Practice comparison: contrast Bitcoin supply rules and settlement design with Ethereum execution, issuance and staking mechanics. Neither profile establishes the better investment, an assured hedge or future upside. Common mistakes with this comparison Treating two token names as proof of diversification. Measure correlation over a stated sample and compare combined exposure under different price shocks. Assuming staking rewards are a guaranteed return. Withdrawal arrangements, validator penalties, service-provider costs and smart-contract risks vary with the method; token-price losses are separate. Treating a lower unit price as proof of cheaper valuation. Units, circulating supply, issuance and the rights associated with an asset are different measures. How to compare a practice worksheet Create separate BTC and ETH columns for transaction validation, network fees, supply changes and custody assumptions. Cite a dated network source for each fact. In a second table, apply the same hypothetical percentage rise and fall to equal starting values, including practice fees. Keep that arithmetic separate from staking income, which TradeHQ does not pay, and from any claim that two tokens provide independent exposures. Add a row distinguishing the simulator transaction fee from a network transaction charge: the former changes virtual cash, while the latter belongs to an external network example. Check whether a quoted network cost uses native units or dollars before comparing it with another network's fee. pages.content: Tesla vs Nvidia Learning notes: Tesla vs Nvidia Tesla reports automotive and energy businesses; NVIDIA sells compute products and supporting software. Tesla reporting separates automotive from energy generation and storage. Those categories suggest different questions: how customers fund compute capacity, how consumers and businesses buy vehicles, and how energy demand affects storage orders. A useful reporting worksheet separates revenue, margin, capital spending and forward-looking statements. Margins: use comparable periods and segment definitions from current company filings rather than fixed percentages. Risk: compare demand, spending, competition and execution assumptions with alternative outcomes. Beta: a beta estimate depends on the benchmark, interval and period; it is not a permanent risk score. pages.content: Bitcoin vs Gold Learning notes: Bitcoin vs Gold Gold and Bitcoin have different ownership, custody and market arrangements. A gold fund also differs from physical gold. Compare specified exposures over matching dates; neither a long history nor a digital supply rule guarantees a hedge. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe.
