How the two differ in practice Gold exposure can mean physical holdings, an exchange-traded fund or a derivative, each with different ownership, custody and cost arrangements. Gold has industrial and reserve uses, but a historical role does not guarantee preservation of purchasing power or gains during market stress. Bitcoin uses a digital network with distinct supply and settlement rules. A comparison should identify the exact exposures and the observation period before describing volatility, demand or correlations; the length of a narrative is not evidence of a reliable hedge. In a hypothetical stress exercise, compare several possible price changes for gold and Bitcoin rather than assume one rises whenever stocks fall. Use equal starting values and record the resulting portfolio contribution, costs and custody assumptions. A recent favourable response does not establish a permanent safe-haven relationship. Different custody methods introduce different operational risks, and neither a price chart nor a simulated return certifies real-money suitability. TradeHQ can illustrate price and portfolio arithmetic without reproducing physical delivery or key custody. Key differences Volatility: compare a specified gold exposure and BTC over the same period and calculation method. Correlation: a relationship with equities depends on the period examined and is not a permanent hedge. Costs: physical custody, fund expenses and crypto key-management arrangements are different and require product-specific checks. Access: trading hours and settlement depend on the instrument, venue and provider; a gold fund is not physical gold. What the comparison shows Practice comparison: contrast physical gold exposure, costs and custody with Bitcoin network and custody risks. Neither is assured currency-crisis insurance or a guarantee of asymmetric upside. Common mistakes with this comparison Assuming equal dollar positions have equal risk. Compare variability and portfolio contributions under stated data and assumptions; no relative position size is prescribed. Calling an asset an inflation hedge from one favorable period. Define the inflation measure, dates and specific exposure before evaluating a relationship; it may change in another sample. Treating a gold fund as physical delivery. Fund expenses, physical storage and Bitcoin custody involve different arrangements and product-specific costs. Read the fund's expense and custody descriptions alongside Bitcoin's transaction and wallet documentation. Compare equal hypothetical starting values under both rising and falling price scenarios, with a separate column for costs excluded by the simulator. pages.description: Apple and Microsoft are both large technology companies, but their business mixes differ.
pages.content: Apple vs Microsoft Learning notes: Apple vs Microsoft Apple and Microsoft are both large technology companies, but their business mixes differ. Apple combines consumer hardware with services and capital returns, while Microsoft combines enterprise software, cloud infrastructure and AI-related products. A useful comparison starts with those business models rather than a short-term price forecast. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. How the two differ in practice Apple's economics combine device sales with recurring services tied to its installed base. When analysing the business, useful questions include how hardware demand changes, how services contribute to revenue and margins, and how dividends or share repurchases affect per-share results. Those figures should be taken from the latest Apple filings because they change over time. Microsoft's economics are heavily connected to enterprise software, subscriptions and cloud infrastructure. Its current reporting also discusses substantial investment in capacity for cloud and AI workloads. When comparing it with Apple, separate revenue growth from the cost of supporting that growth and use the latest Microsoft filings for current rates, spending and segment definitions. Use comparable reporting periods when comparing growth, margins and cash returns. Key differences Revenue mix: compare Apple's hardware and services contribution with Microsoft's productivity, cloud and other enterprise businesses. AI exposure: compare how each company describes AI-related products, infrastructure spending and monetisation in its current filings. Capital return: both companies return cash to shareholders; check current dividends, repurchases and share-count changes in their latest reports. Regulation: both operate under changing competition, platform, privacy and technology rules, so use current filings rather than a permanent regulatory label. What the comparison shows Practice comparison: examine Apple's hardware, services and capital-return model alongside Microsoft's enterprise software, cloud and AI-infrastructure model. Neither profile is automatically the better investment; the relevant risks and valuation assumptions differ. Common mistakes with this comparison Treating a mega-cap company as low risk simply because it is large. Large companies can still experience substantial drawdowns and business-model changes. Comparing headline per-share metrics without checking share-count changes, capital spending and cash returns. Those factors can alter what per-share growth means. Assuming an index position gives the same exposure for every investor. If you are comparing a single stock with an index fund, check the fund's current holdings and weights first. How to compare a practice worksheet Use Apple and Microsoft filings from comparable reporting periods. Record hardware/services and enterprise/cloud segment definitions, capital spending and share-count changes. Mark any metric that cannot be compared directly. How the two differ in practice A network comparison should identify where execution happens and how results are verified. Ethereum's scaling documentation discusses layer-2 rollups with different security models; a mainnet transaction and a rollup transaction should not be counted interchangeably. A comparison can examine where fees are charged, how supply changes and which security assumptions apply without presuming that greater activity raises price. Staking rewards are denominated in the token and can be affected by costs, issuance, protocol rules and market-price losses. Comparing nominal reward percentages alone does not establish an inflation-adjusted investment return. Document the source and period and separate the network’s design from a forecast of its token’s value. Key differences Throughput: define transaction type, observation period and inclusion of votes or rollup activity before comparing counts. Fees: actual fees vary with transaction type and network conditions; no fixed cost range is established here. Reliability: compare documented incidents and their dates rather than claim that a network has never halted. Staking: rewards, issuance, fees and operational risks differ; advertised yield is not a guaranteed real return. Observed throughput, congestion and reliability must be compared using consistent definitions. Reading a token reward percentage as a cash return. State the period, token-price change, fees, penalties and supply assumptions; subtracting issuance alone does not calculate an investor's return. Predicting a token-price response from an outage. Record the incident's date, duration and affected services separately from any claim about adoption or price. Record whether Ethereum activity is on mainnet or a named layer 2, what each transaction count includes, how confirmation is defined and when fees were measured. How the two differ in practice A EUR/USD quote expresses dollars per euro; a stock price expresses currency per share. Neither unit should be confused with the whole account's return. Currency research can examine dated policy and economic information, while stock research can examine company reports, but neither approach guarantees a dependable price response. A pair can trend or fluctuate over a selected period; it has no obligation to return to a chosen average. Identify the instrument and calculation units before comparing outcomes. Leverage increases gains and losses relative to the funds committed, and requirements depend on the product, jurisdiction and provider. A quoted price’s usual daily range does not establish a safe leverage level or explain a universal share of account losses. For a learning exercise, compare hypothetical unleveraged exposures and record how a price shock changes account value. TradeHQ uses simplified spot practice, so it does not reproduce a margin agreement, forced liquidation or every currency execution condition. Key differences Turnover: any comparison needs a dated survey and matching definitions; no permanent daily dollar total is asserted here. Leverage: permitted leverage depends on jurisdiction, product and provider, and does not establish appropriate exposure. Hours: currency and equity venue schedules, holidays and extended-hours arrangements differ. Analysis: macroeconomic and company information can inform hypotheses without establishing a dependable trading edge. What the comparison shows Practice comparison: distinguish relative currency prices from company ownership and cash flows. Neither instrument category guarantees wealth compounding or suits every short-term trader. Common mistakes with this comparison Treating available leverage or a stop distance as proof of safety. A stop trigger does not guarantee execution at a chosen price; TradeHQ does not place resting stops or model margin contracts. Inferring a real news reaction from a simulated chart. A scheduled release needs dated external observations and venue conditions to support an event study. Confusing quote units with company ownership. Currency appreciation and retained company earnings describe different mechanisms; neither guarantees an account gain. How to compare a practice worksheet Choose a named pair such as EUR/USD and a named equity such as AAPL from the practice terminal. Write dollars per euro and dollars per share next to their hypothetical prices, then calculate quantity times price using those units. Apply positive and negative price changes without leverage. pages.content: Learn Bitcoin — Virtual Practice Learning notes: Learn Bitcoin — Virtual Practice Bitcoin is a digital asset with a protocol-defined issuance schedule. Its market price is separate from that schedule and can change without a protocol change. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Understanding Bitcoin Begin with the difference between coin return and account return. A hypothetical 10% BTC rise applied to a $10,000 holding adds $1,000 before costs, while an otherwise cash-only $100,000 account rises only 1%. The same headline percentage can therefore describe a much larger asset move than portfolio move. Factors to distinguish when studying the instrument Compare the protocol supply schedule, exchange trading activity and news claims as separate sources of information. A halving event does not by itself determine the direction or timing of a price change. Compare a dated primary description of Bitcoin with the practice chart. A simulated movement is not evidence that a particular news item changed the real market price. Step by step Compare the coin’s percentage change with whole-account return using cash and holding values. Visit /trade/btc and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance. Using a hypothetical BTC holding of 0.05 units at $50,000 per unit, calculate $2,500 of virtual exposure and a $2.50 entry fee at the simulator's 0.1% rate; then compare with the displayed practice quote. Record the dated BTC quote and an alternative 10% down-price case. For the same 0.05 BTC, that implies a $250 gross holding loss before fees, not a 10% loss of the whole $100,000 account. Create a second BTC price scenario with the same unit count so gross holding return and total-account return can be compared. Worked hypothetical accounting example Use a hypothetical $100,000 account with $90,000 cash and a $10,000 BTC holding before fees. A selected 10% BTC rise takes the holding to $11,000 and total value to $101,000, before excluded costs. The asset return is 10%; account return is 1%. The current holding weight is $11,000 ÷ $101,000 = about 10.89%, not 11% of the original balance. If the $10,000 purchase incurred the simulator’s 0.1% fee, cash would instead be $89,990 and total marked equity $100,990. These inputs teach accounting rather than recommend exposure. Timing and liquidity Compare BTC’s provider observation timestamp with the chart’s source label. A periodically refreshed reference can differ from a venue’s last trade or a different-minute quote without proving either is fraudulent. Save the observation time used in your worksheet so that a later account change can be reconstructed. Opening the page is not an exchange fill. Mistakes specific to this instrument Reporting the BTC return as the entire account return despite a large cash balance. Calculating new allocation with the original account denominator. Calling an aggregate provider mark a reserved exchange fill. Ignoring both buy and sell fees in the result. Reviewing the worksheet Write the position’s percentage move, dollar change and whole-account return on separate lines. Recompute allocation using the new total. Then reconcile fees and inspect observation age. This review can help distinguish an asset's movement from the account return and preserve unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Risk BTC price risk and quote-data risk are distinct. A correctly identified asset can still have an older provider observation; a recent page fetch does not make that observation current. A small BTC weight can limit its contribution to one assumed account move, but it cannot prevent the holding from losing value. Real execution is not reproduced by a paper mark. If you are learning from outside the US A short BTC study session can focus on one unit conversion: coin quantity × dollars per coin. Keep virtual accounting separate from questions about real wallets, local access or funding. The practice account holds no real coins and makes no on-chain transfer; current eligibility and tax questions belong to official local information. pages.content: Learn Ethereum — Virtual Practice Learning notes: Learn Ethereum — Virtual Practice Ethereum is a network for running applications and smart contracts; ether, or ETH, is its native currency. People use ETH to pay network fees, transfer value and participate in staking. Trading ETH means exchanging that currency at a market price. TradeHQ lets you practise the price and quantity calculations with virtual funds; it does not send coins to a wallet or stake them. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Understanding Ethereum Separate the network from the currency: Ethereum is the system, while ETH is the unit whose price you see. A lower price per coin than BTC does not by itself mean ETH is cheaper in valuation terms. Factors to distinguish when studying the instrument Network use and ETH price measure different things. Gas is the unit used to measure transaction work; the network fee is paid in ETH. A busy network can change fees without producing a matching percentage change in the exchange price. Staking helps secure Ethereum, while layer-two networks handle activity with a different fee structure. These concepts explain how the network works; a TradeHQ price chart does not measure staking rewards, network demand or the effect of a particular headline. Step by step Identify ether (ETH) as Ethereum’s native currency. Read the ETH/USD quote, its timestamp and the source before considering a hypothetical order; an indicative price is not a guaranteed execution price. Visit /trade/eth and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance. Use 0.5 ETH at an illustrative $3,200 quote to calculate $1,600 of virtual exposure and a $1.60 simulator entry fee. That is separate from real blockchain gas charges, which TradeHQ does not execute. Record a second hypothetical ETH price and calculate the change for the same 0.5 ETH. Check the page's quote timestamp; a price screenshot cannot reveal the gas or exchange costs of a real transfer. For the fictional example, review changes in ETH units, cash and simulator fees. Keep real Ethereum network gas and staking separate: TradeHQ neither transfers nor stakes coins. Worked hypothetical accounting example For a hypothetical buy of 2 ETH at $2,500 per ETH, notional is $5,000 and the simulator’s 0.1% purchase fee is $5. The cash debit is $5,005. If the later quote is $2,400, the marked holding is $4,800, giving a $200 price loss and $205 equity reduction after the purchase fee. A sale at that quote would add a $4.80 exit fee. A separately quoted blockchain gas fee is not a simulator cost: this paper buy did not create a network transaction or send ETH to a wallet. Timing and liquidity A provider can aggregate ETH market observations while a blockchain explorer describes network activity. Match the question to the source: exchange-price timestamps for paper valuation, network records for transaction mechanics. Do not use a synthetic practice candle as evidence that a gas-fee change caused a real price reaction. Mistakes specific to this instrument Adding a real blockchain gas charge to a paper buy that sent no coins. Describing virtual ETH as staked funds earning rewards. Comparing whole-coin prices as if they establish relative business valuation. Mixing dollar loss with loss per ETH unit. Reviewing the worksheet After the exercise, reconcile ETH units, notional cost, simulator fee and cash separately. If the quote moves $100 per ETH and you own 2 ETH, the gross marked change is $200. A gas-charge discussion belongs in a separate network worksheet. Check that neither staking income nor a wallet transfer was invented in the virtual ledger. Risk Network fees, staking mechanics and ETH market-price exposure are different risks and activities. TradeHQ illustrates only the supported virtual spot accounting; it does not stake ETH, transfer coins or pay staking rewards. A correct network explanation cannot establish which direction the market price will move. Include the actual simulator fees when assessing a paper outcome. If you are learning from outside the US Use this guide to learn the difference between Ethereum as a network and ETH as a unit. A classroom example can compare exchange fees and hypothetical network charges without funding a wallet. Local real-asset access, eligibility and taxes require current official sources; a simulator lesson is not permission to transact. Educational simulation only — not financial advice. pages.content: Learn Nvidia — Virtual Practice Learning notes: Learn Nvidia — Virtual Practice Nvidia supplies computing products and services. Its share price and its operating business are different objects: a change in sales does not translate mechanically into the same percentage stock return. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Understanding Nvidia Separate company operating measures from the share-price return. A hypothetical 20% sales increase and a 5% stock decline can coexist when expectations, costs or guidance differ. The price observation alone does not tell you which explanation is correct. Factors to distinguish when studying the instrument Company results, customer spending statements, supply constraints and export rules can provide business context. Verify any current figures from dated primary reports; none of these topics establishes that a trend-following strategy will outperform. Compare a dated primary description of Nvidia with the practice chart. A simulated movement is not evidence that a particular news item changed the real market price. Step by step List direct company exposure and any assumed fund overlap before computing the combined account weight. Visit /trade/nvda and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance. Using five hypothetical NVDA shares at $120 each, calculate a $600 virtual position and $0.60 simulated entry fee. Do not treat the worksheet price as a live quotation. Record any NVDA weight already held inside a chosen ETF using that fund's dated holdings report, then combine direct and indirect exposure before interpreting an illustrative price change. Compare direct NVIDIA shares with a hypothetical dated ETF allocation to identify potential overlap before interpreting a percentage change. Worked hypothetical accounting example Imagine a $10,000 worksheet with $2,000 held directly in NVDA and $8,000 in a fund. Assume, only for this exercise, that the fund has a 10% NVDA weight. The indirect exposure is $800, so combined NVDA exposure is $2,800, or 28% of total value. Counting two account rows misses this overlap. A selected 10% NVDA fall contributes $280 of loss through the two exposures using the initial exposures and assuming other holdings stay unchanged. Real fund weights need a dated holdings source; the assumed 10% is not a current portfolio fact. Timing and liquidity Distinguish a dated financial statement, guidance and an intraday price quote. They answer different questions and update on different schedules. A synthetic chart cannot validate a claim about customer demand. In a report exercise, write what the market was expected to learn as well as what the company announced. Mistakes specific to this instrument Counting a fund and direct shares as wholly independent exposures. Using an undated assumed fund weight as a current fact. Assuming a sales-growth percentage dictates the stock-return percentage. Inferring fair value from the nominal price of one share. Reviewing the worksheet Review both the direct holding and any assumed fund overlap. Record whether fund weights were actual dated inputs or deliberately hypothetical. Recompute the account denominator after price changes, and separate operating metrics from share-price results. The goal is a reproducible exposure explanation, not a claim that two technology labels imply diversification. Risk Direct NVDA shares can overlap a technology or broad-market fund you also hold. Row count is therefore an incomplete diversification measure. Inspect actual fund weights and their dates before computing look-through exposure. Company sales growth and diversification labels do not guarantee protection from losses or a positive share-price response. Twenty $50 units and two $500 units both make $1,000 positions before fees. Factors to distinguish when studying the instrument Fund holdings, index methodology, distributions and expenses describe the instrument. Consult current fund documents for those details. An index comparison can be a benchmark, but a short practice sample cannot prove an investing strategy is better. Compare a dated primary description of S&P 500 ETF with the practice chart. A simulated movement is not evidence that a particular news item changed the real market price. Step by step Identify fund units and current account weight; label any distribution or fund-expense concepts not simulated. Visit /trade/spy and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance. For two illustrative SPY units at $500 each, calculate $1,000 of virtual fund exposure and a $1 simulated entry fee. Keep the unit price distinct from the fund's constituent-stock prices. Calculate the combined account weight of this $1,000 fund exposure and any direct shares that overlap its disclosed holdings; note that distributions, expense ratios and full tracking effects are not modelled in the basic virtual order. Label how the ETF's distribution and operating costs are outside the simplified practice order, and calculate exposure against total account value. Worked hypothetical accounting example A hypothetical SPY worksheet holds ten units at $500, or $5,000, while the account has $95,000 cash before purchase fees. A selected 2% price decline changes the holding to $4,900: a $100 price loss, or 0.1% of the original $100,000 account. The simulator purchase fee on $5,000 is $5. If marked at the lower quote after that fee, equity would be $99,895. Fund-level holdings, distributions and expenses are separate concepts; this simple paper mark does not reproduce a complete fund accounting statement. Timing and liquidity A recently fetched fund quote can still refer to an earlier market observation, particularly outside the relevant session. Read the source and observation time rather than calling a weekend page refresh a new trade. The simulator’s chart status also determines whether candles are provider history or synthetic practice inputs. Ignoring overlap between the fund and separately held company shares. Inventing a cash distribution that the simulator did not record. Explain how the $100 holding loss becomes a much smaller account percentage because most of this worksheet is cash. Include fees and note any distribution or expense mechanics excluded from the simulator rather than silently inventing cash entries. Risk A broad fund can reduce exposure to one company while remaining exposed to market losses and overlap with direct stocks. Diversification is not immunity. Actual fund constituents and weights require dated disclosures, and a fixed index name does not establish that every constituent contributes equally to your result. pages.content: Learn Solana — Virtual Practice Learning notes: Learn Solana — Virtual Practice SOL is Solana's native token, while Solana is the network on which SOL is used for transaction fees. Learning to read a SOL price quote is not the same as transferring SOL on-chain, staking tokens or trading a derivatives contract. TradeHQ offers a virtual spot-price practice exercise only. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Understanding Solana The simulated SOL holding represents exposure to token-price changes, not ownership in Solana Labs or an entitlement to network revenue. Network transaction fees paid in SOL, token-staking mechanics and the cost of buying or selling SOL on an exchange are distinct concepts. The TradeHQ spot simulation does not perform blockchain transactions or staking. Factors to distinguish when studying the instrument Read Solana's primary documentation to distinguish network transaction processing and fee mechanics from exchange spot trading. Usage and technology changes may matter to market participants, but they do not determine a particular SOL price or return. Compare two dated, clearly identified price observations before calculating a percentage change. Network or ecosystem news may coincide with price movements without demonstrating that it caused them. Step by step Identify the instrument before doing any arithmetic: SOL is the token, a SOL/USD quote is a price per token, and an exchange venue's quoted price may differ from a separate source. Record the quote currency, source and observation time. Choose a hypothetical dollar budget and SOL unit price. Divide budget by unit price to calculate units, then add the simulator's stated 0.1% virtual order fee to estimate cash required. Use amounts solely for the worksheet, not as a recommended allocation. On /trade/sol, inspect the quoted spot price and any data-status label. No order is required for this worksheet; the simulator does not support resting limit or stop orders, short positions or staking. Write two different exit-price scenarios before reading a later quote. Calculate gross profit or loss as units times the change in dollars per SOL; subtract hypothetical buy and sell transaction fees separately. Review what the exercise could and could not show: quote observation versus actual fill, changes in SOL value versus whole-portfolio return, and missing real-world exchange costs, spread, slippage and custody. Worked hypothetical accounting example Hypothetical example, not live market data: suppose SOL is $125 and the practice order is 40 SOL. The gross purchase value is 40 × $125 = $5,000; a 0.1% virtual buy fee is $5. If the later assumed price is $130, gross marked value is 40 × $130 = $5,200 and the gross change is $200. A hypothetical sale at $130 with a further 0.1% simulator fee of $5.20 would make the round-trip result $189.80 before any costs not simulated. If SOL instead fell to $115, the holding would be worth $4,600: a $400 gross decline before fees. These are chosen numbers, not a forecast or a liquidity guarantee. Timing and liquidity Digital-asset venues may operate around the clock, but 24/7 access does not mean identical liquidity at every moment. Compare source timestamp, spreads and event conditions when studying external market data. TradeHQ's chart can be sourced differently from its quote; inspect the data labels and avoid treating a chart candle as proof that a real-world market order would fill at that exact price. Mistakes specific to this instrument Confusing an exchange SOL price with the on-chain fee for sending a Solana transaction. Using a marked portfolio value as if it were a guaranteed executable sale price. Ignoring the second virtual fee when calculating a hypothetical round trip. Assuming network usage or a technical announcement guarantees token-price appreciation. Reviewing the worksheet Record the hypothetical buy and sell prices, quantity, both virtual fees, source timestamps and portfolio allocation. Separate token return from total-account return and note which slippage, spread and custody costs the simulation omits. Try a lower exit-price case as well as a higher one to test the same arithmetic. Risk SOL's token price can move rapidly in either direction. Exchange liquidity, order size, spread and execution terms affect an actual fill; network reliability and token supply information do not predict the next price. In a simulator, a displayed mark and a later virtual fill may not recreate exchange execution or custody risk. Never equate a hypothetical outcome with achievable returns. Laws and access conditions vary by jurisdiction; a financial-education worksheet is not confirmation that a venue or product is available locally. Educational simulation only — not financial advice. pages.description: Learn how Scalping works, then practise it with $100,000 virtual cash.
pages.content: Scalping Learning notes: Scalping A step-by-step walkthrough of Scalping with practice on the free $100,000 simulator. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What it is A short-horizon price and transaction-cost comparison; no fixed interval defines the concept. Scalping describes attempts to capture small changes over short intervals. Because the intended price change is small, a spread, fee or execution delay can form a large part of the result. A two-tick cost is 20% of a ten-tick gross target, but that ratio does not establish expected profit: win frequency, adverse outcomes and all costs would also be needed. Market conditions that matter Liquidity and spreads vary by venue, instrument, session and event. A small spread observed in one period is not a permanent property or a reliable profit opportunity. Compare observations over stated dates rather than assign universally favorable trading hours. Study context A study of how spreads, fees and latency affect short-horizon calculations; not a suitability recommendation. Limitations Simplified fills and generated candles do not reproduce order-book priority, partial fills or intraday liquidity. The steps Choose one instrument and explicitly fictional entry, exit and cost inputs for a short-horizon worksheet. State the chart interval and whether the observations are provider history or generated practice candles. Calculate the effect of a worse fill and a wider spread before comparing gains and losses. Record all selected cases, including unfavorable ones. TradeHQ supports manual market orders; planned stops are worksheet assumptions. Worked example Hypothetical one-BTC worksheet: buy at $95,120 and compare exits at $95,210 and $95,080. Before costs, these are a $90 gain and a $40 loss. At TradeHQ's 0.1% fee on each side, the entry fee is $95.12. Selling at $95,210 adds a $95.21 fee, turning the gross gain into a $100.33 net loss. Selling at $95,080 adds a $95.08 fee, making the net loss $230.20. The exit prices are assumptions, not resting stop or target orders; a real fill can differ. The numbers behind it For the same one-BTC example, cash paid is $95,120 × 1.001 = $95,215.12. Net sale proceeds at $95,210 are $95,210 × 0.999 = $95,114.79, so the round-trip result is −$100.33. The fee-only break-even exit solves exit price × 0.999 = $95,215.12, or approximately $95,310.43 before any additional costs. A higher assumed win rate cannot make this selected $95,210 exit profitable after those fees. These are hypothetical prices, not a return forecast. How it fails Comparing a gross target with a result after fees as if they were the same measure. Treating a generated candle as evidence of an actual order-book fill. Changing size or exit assumptions after seeing the result and combining the changed rule with the original sample. Scope and source limitations No universal win rate or sufficient sample size applies. Recorded hypothetical outcomes depend on the sample design, assumptions and costs. pages.content: Swing Trading Learning notes: Swing Trading A step-by-step walkthrough of Swing Trading with practice on the free $100,000 simulator. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What it is A comparison of multi-session price observations and overnight exposure. Swing trading describes positions held across sessions, often over days or weeks. The label does not determine a suitable position size or make the decision less consequential. A scheduled review can fit some learners’ routines, but holdings remain exposed between observations and suitability cannot be inferred from employment status. Overnight gaps are possible when information arrives between sessions; a worksheet threshold is not an execution guarantee. Market conditions that matter An apparent trend or pullback is a description of selected past data. A later continuation and a reversal are both possible. Earnings and other announcements can introduce overnight gaps; a planned exit does not guarantee a fill at that price. Study context A worksheet comparing multi-day observation windows and overnight exposure; no work schedule establishes suitability. Limitations Manual review leaves exposure between observations, and an intended exit can be crossed by a gap. The steps Define a multi-day observation window without implying that a holding period predicts a return. Record a hypothetical entry, quantity and exit assumption before examining later observations. Compare different gap sizes and exit distances, including an unfilled or worse-than-planned exit. Keep fixed, partial and trailing exit rules in separate conceptual comparisons. TradeHQ does not place automatic stops. Worked example In a fictional multi-session price series, compare an initial observation with a later higher observation and a later lower observation. A price gap can cross an assumed review threshold. Neither a threshold nor a selected favorable case establishes actual execution or likely returns. The numbers behind it Hypothetical arithmetic: fixed realized 47% wins at 2R and 53% losses at 1R give 0.41R gross expectancy per trade. With an arbitrary $1,000 practice loss amount, that is $410 before costs. These assumed inputs do not establish performance. Losing-run probabilities require a sample length and independence assumption; no particular run is guaranteed or universally normal. How it fails Treating a round-number exit or volatility multiple as guaranteed loss protection. Assuming favorable earnings or a company narrative determines the next opening price. Adding to a position while reporting results as though exposure had stayed fixed. Scope and source limitations The distribution of a hypothetical sample depends on its dates, observation rules, costs and assumptions. TradeHQ does not validate a method's performance. pages.content: Day Trading Learning notes: Day Trading A step-by-step walkthrough of Day Trading with practice on the free $100,000 simulator. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What it is Opening and closing all positions within a single session. Day trading usually means opening and closing positions within the same trading day. If a position is fully closed, it has no later overnight exposure, but an intended close is not guaranteed during a halt, outage or loss of liquidity. A short holding period does not make a position low risk. Frequency, costs, execution and behavior all affect the outcome. Market conditions that matter Ranges, spreads and traded volumes differ across sessions and events. Selecting only sessions that later looked favorable creates selection bias. A meaningful comparison records its dates, includes unfavorable cases and uses information available before each hypothetical decision. Study context A study of same-session accounting and transaction costs, rather than a recommendation for full-time activity. Limitations Repeated orders add costs and operational demands. Closing by a chosen time is an assumption that can fail during a halt or outage. The steps Define a hypothetical session window and identify the relevant venue and calendar. State an entry and exit rule in advance, using only calculations available in the chosen data source. Calculate how repeated fees and worse fills change the same gross price outcome. Record whether the hypothetical exit occurred. Do not assume an outage or trading halt permits a closing transaction. Worked example In a fictional same-session dataset, compare an observed price with its volume-weighted average and with another observation later in the session. Compare positive and negative differences, then record the extra cost of repeated transactions. No indicator-based order is required. The numbers behind it Hypothetical arithmetic: fixed realized 52% wins at 1.5R and 48% losses at 1R give 0.30R gross expectancy. An arbitrary 0.5% of $100,000 is $500, so expectancy is $150 per trade and $750 across five trades before costs. This is an input-based worksheet, not observed returns or a slippage estimate. How it fails Assuming a particular hour or chart pattern guarantees a favorable range. Presenting an intended stop or session loss threshold as an enforced maximum loss. Inferring a trader’s emotional state or the next outcome from the number of recent losing trades. Scope and source limitations There is no dependable universal win-rate range. Evaluate the method by expectancy, drawdown, costs and consistency across a larger sample. Educational simulation only — not financial advice. pages.description: Learn how Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) works, then practise it with $100,000 virtual cash.
pages.content: Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) Learning notes: Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) A step-by-step walkthrough of Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) with practice on the free $100,000 simulator. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What it is Investing equal amounts on a predetermined schedule rather than selecting each purchase date based on a price prediction. Dollar-cost averaging describes a recurring cash-flow rule, not a method that removes market timing risk. The schedule reduces decisions about individual purchase dates, but entry prices and the investment's ultimate value remain uncertain. It is particularly important to distinguish gradual access to savings from choosing to hold already-available cash for later purchases. Market conditions that matter In a steadily rising example market, earlier investment of already-available cash can outperform staggered entries because more units participate in the rise. On a falling path, staggered purchases can sometimes produce a lower average entry price, but both schedules can lose money. Any comparison must use the same asset, end date, fees and funding assumptions; cherry-picked price paths are not evidence of expected performance. Study context A classroom comparison of repeated contributions and lump-sum purchase schedules, with equal total funding and clearly stated cash-availability dates. Limitations DCA does not prevent loss, make an unsafe investment suitable, or outperform a lump sum consistently; transaction fees can accumulate. The steps Choose an entirely hypothetical instrument, a purchase calendar and a fixed cash contribution. At each assumed date, divide the contribution by the unit price to calculate units. If fees apply, subtract the fee from the cash available for units. Add contributions and units, then calculate average cost per unit as total purchase cost divided by units acquired; this is a historical accounting figure, not a future-value estimate. Compare the final market value against total contributions at the same end date, using a separate scenario where the full amount was available from the start. Discuss access to funds, costs, permanent-loss risk and what would happen if purchases stopped early; no schedule guarantees a profit. Worked example Hypothetical fee-free worksheet: contribute $100 when the unit prices are $10, $8 and $12. The purchases acquire 10, 12.5 and about 8.333 units respectively, or about 30.833 units for $300. At the final $12 price they are worth approximately $370, a $70 unrealized gain before any costs. A $300 lump sum at the initial $10 price, if all funds had been available then, buys 30 units worth $360 at the end. This one invented path cannot establish which schedule performs better generally. The numbers behind it In the fee-free three-date example, unit total = $100/$10 + $100/$8 + $100/$12 = approximately 30.8333 units. Historical average cash paid per unit = $300/30.8333 = approximately $9.73. At a final quoted $12, marked value ≈ $370 and gain ≈ $70. An alternative $300 lump sum at $10 acquires 30 units with marked value $360. Change the price sequence and the comparison may reverse; no realistic return estimate is implied. How it fails Describing DCA as a guarantee of a lower average entry price or positive returns. Comparing a lump sum invested on day one with periodic savings that were not available on day one. Overlooking transaction fees, uninvested cash and the possibility of permanent impairment. Scope and source limitations Measure adherence to a schedule separately from returns. Outcomes depend on the path of prices, fee terms, what was purchased and when cash was actually available. Educational simulation only — not financial advice. pages.content: RSI Mean-Reversion Learning notes: RSI Mean-Reversion A step-by-step walkthrough of RSI Mean-Reversion with practice on the free $100,000 simulator. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What it is A conceptual comparison of RSI thresholds and later price observations. RSI compares smoothed recent gains and losses over a selected lookback and scales the result between zero and 100. Fourteen periods is a common setting; the interval must also be stated. Conventional threshold labels describe the calculation. They do not establish that an asset is mispriced or that a price reversal must follow. Market conditions that matter RSI can remain extreme during a sustained move or cross its thresholds repeatedly. Comparing samples labeled trending and ranging requires a rule for those labels that does not use future information. A second indicator shares price inputs and is not necessarily independent confirmation. Study context Studying how the same oscillator threshold behaves in different historical samples. Limitations An extreme reading can persist. Neither a threshold nor a second chart pattern proves a reversal. The steps Specify a standard RSI calculation and interval using a source that supplies the necessary historical prices. Mark the conventional 30 and 70 thresholds as descriptions, then record all observations meeting them. Compare later continuation and reversal cases under the same sampling and cost assumptions. Treat entry and exit choices as separate hypothetical rules. TradeHQ’s RSI-style practice value is not a standard historical RSI calculation. Worked example In a fictional price dataset, an oscillator crosses a selected descriptive threshold. Compare a later continuation and a later reversal. Neither the reading nor a candlestick label establishes a price prediction or an instruction to transact. The numbers behind it Hypothetical comparison: fixed realized 57% wins at 1.2R and 43% losses at 1R give 0.254R gross expectancy. Changing only the assumed win rate to 32% gives 0.32×1.2−0.68=−0.296R. These chosen inputs do not establish the observed profitability of ranging or trending markets; costs and actual fills must also be considered. How it fails Treating an oscillator threshold as a mandatory buy or sell instruction. Assuming a candlestick pattern proves a reversal or that simulated volume validates it. Selecting lookbacks after seeing profitable historical outcomes without testing a separate sample. Scope and source limitations RSI-based results can vary sharply by market regime and rule set. Test the same rules in ranging and trending periods rather than relying on a fixed win-rate claim. Educational simulation only — not financial advice. pages.content: MACD Crossover Learning notes: MACD Crossover A step-by-step walkthrough of MACD Crossover with practice on the free $100,000 simulator. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. What it is A conceptual study of historical indicator crossings and their limitations. MACD subtracts a 26-period exponential moving average from a 12-period average and compares the result with a 9-period signal line. These historical inputs create lag. A crossover can persist or reverse; the calculation does not establish a win rate, profitability or how many false starts a rule filters. Market conditions that matter A sustained historical move and a sideways sample can produce different numbers of crossovers. That observation does not prove a universally favorable asset class or timeframe. A filter based on a longer average is another rule to test with the same data and costs, rather than an established improvement. For a concrete comparison, label a five-bar sequence of hypothetical MACD values and identify exactly which bar produces a crossover rather than drawing a line after seeing the outcome. Record whether the signal was calculated at bar close or while the bar was still forming; that difference can alter whether a crossing appears at all. When calculated from closing prices alone, the indicator does not directly incorporate bid-ask spreads, execution priority or transaction fees. Study context Studying differences between moving averages, signal-line crossings and alternative exit assumptions. Limitations Lag and repeated crossings can create unfavorable hypothetical outcomes; no market regime guarantees performance. The steps Specify the price series, interval and EMA calculation; 12, 26 and 9 are conventional settings, not validated defaults. Record each selected signal-line crossing without discarding later unfavorable cases. Choose fictional entry and exit assumptions before calculating results, including a case where price moves before entry. Compare costs and alternative rules in a worksheet. TradeHQ does not provide a MACD overlay or genuine short selling. Worked example In a fictional indicator sequence, mark a crossing and compare two alternative subsequent price paths. A selected favorable path is not an observed return, an execution guarantee or a rule for an actual order. The numbers behind it Hypothetical arithmetic: fixed realized 43% wins at 2.5R and 57% losses at 1R give 0.505R gross expectancy before costs. A planned reward-to-risk ratio is not the realized payoff. Losing-run probabilities depend on sample length, independence and the assumed win rate; a six-to-eight-loss run is not a universally expected outcome. How it fails Reporting only favorable crossings while excluding costly reversals. Treating a planned reward-to-risk ratio as a realized payoff. Assuming histogram divergence establishes a reversal or a profitable trade. Scope and source limitations MACD results vary by timeframe, market and exit rule. pages.content: Trading Strategies Learning notes: Trading Strategies Compare six strategy topics through conceptual worksheets and supported spot practice with $100,000 in virtual cash. No strategy performance is validated. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Named strategy walkthroughs The directory compares six different educational topics. Short-horizon methods, multi-day methods, indicator exercises and fixed-schedule purchases serve different questions. Examples use hypothetical inputs, not documented live performance. Read each method's limitations and supporting references before interpreting a calculation. Strategies covered Scalping — A short-horizon price and transaction-cost comparison; no fixed interval defines the concept. Swing Trading — A comparison of multi-session price observations and overnight exposure. Day Trading — Opening and closing all positions within a single session. Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) — Investing equal amounts on a predetermined schedule rather than selecting each purchase date based on a price prediction. RSI Mean-Reversion — A conceptual comparison of RSI thresholds and later price observations. MACD Crossover — A conceptual study of historical indicator crossings and their limitations. A simple comparison before choosing a worksheet Consider two different teaching questions: a fixed $100 contribution made at three specified dates is a cash-flow exercise, whereas recording a MACD crossing on three observations is an indicator-definition exercise. They do not use the same denominator or imply comparable expected returns. For the contribution exercise, list total cash added and total units; for an indicator exercise, state the source, price interval and calculation before counting any signals. Neither example needs a live trade. The choice of an exercise should follow the concept being studied, not a claim that a holding period or indicator offers a better outcome. Any comparison of observed results needs consistent date ranges, costs, valuation conventions and a clear statement that a selected sample cannot verify future performance. What a strategy is, and what it is not A trading rule describes a testable set of conditions and assumptions. Dollar-cost averaging is different: it schedules contributions, without requiring an active entry or exit signal. The site presents these methods for comparison, not as advice about which method is suitable for a person. A chosen win percentage without the payoff distribution and costs is not enough to evaluate outcomes. Results from a selected historical or virtual sample are descriptive; they may change in another sample. No source-backed universal winning percentage or account-return forecast is offered. Testing a strategy without fooling yourself Write down the hypothetical assumptions and observation window before reviewing outcomes. Avoid treating 30, 100 or any other arbitrary number of observations as a universal statistical threshold. Sample design, selection and dependence matter. Record cases selected by the exercise criteria, including unfavorable cases and changes to the rule. If using sample expectancy or drawdown, explicitly label the costs, sizes, dates and limitations of the input data. Check the effect of a negative-outcome sequence without asserting how often it will occur in practice. Compare a second specified sample without claiming that a backtest establishes future results. pages.content: What Is an Option? Calls & Puts Explained Learning notes: What Is an Option? Calls & Puts Explained A stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Summary A stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves. The core definition This lesson focuses on standard unadjusted US equity options, which generally cover 100 shares. A call gives its buyer a right to buy and a put a right to sell at the strike under the contract terms. American-style options can be exercised before expiry; European-style options have a different exercise schedule. Adjusted contracts and cash-settled index options can have different deliverables. The writer takes the corresponding obligation. Read the specific contract and OCC risk disclosure rather than assume every option is identical. For a standard unadjusted 100-share contract, the quoted premium is stated per share. An option premium depends on multiple pricing inputs, including the underlying price, strike, remaining time, implied volatility, interest rates and dividends. It is not a direct measure of an individual participant's expectations. Why options exist A share holder can buy a put to offset some losses below its strike during the option term, at the cost of its premium. A covered call adds premium income but limits upside and retains substantial share-price risk. These examples illustrate different payoffs; neither is a guaranteed return or a universally suitable position. A simple worked example Imagine Apple trades at $180 and you buy one 30-day $185 call for $3.00 ($300 total). Three things can happen. If Apple closes above $188 on expiration, you're profitable — the intrinsic value of the call exceeds what you paid. An expiration price strictly between $185 and $188 gives the call intrinsic value but a net loss before costs; $188 is gross break-even. If it closes at or below $185, the call expires worthless and you lose the full $300 — but nothing more. These are hypothetical expiration payoffs before costs for the purchased option alone. Exercise can create a stock position with separate funding and market risk. Short options have different obligations, and an uncovered short call can have unlimited loss. What you can practise on TradeHQ TradeHQ supports spot instruments, including shares and ETFs, with $100,000 virtual capital. It does not model option strikes, expirations or premiums. Use this lesson's worked examples to calculate hypothetical contract payoffs on paper; buying an underlying share in the simulator is a different transaction from buying an option on it. > Options are contracts, not shares. Time value generally erodes as expiry approaches, but the total premium can rise or fall with other pricing inputs. (Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) Key takeaways A standard unadjusted US equity option generally covers 100 shares; adjusted and other contracts can differ. At expiration, before costs, a purchased call has a net gain above strike + premium; a purchased put has a net gain below strike − premium. Those levels are break-even prices. A purchased option held without exercise can lose its premium plus costs; exercise can create a separate underlying position and obligations. Options can be used for hedging and speculation; their risk depends on the position and contract. Check your understanding How many shares does one standard US equity option contract control? Options: 10; 50; 100; 1,000. Correct answer: 100. Why: A standard unadjusted US equity option generally covers 100 shares. Adjusted deliverables and other option types differ. What is the maximum loss for someone who buys (goes long) a single call option? Options: Unlimited; The strike price × 100; The premium paid; The stock price × 100. Correct answer: The premium paid. Why: For the purchased option alone before exercise and costs, loss is limited to the premium. Exercise can create a separate position. A call option gives the buyer the right to: Options: Sell shares at the strike price; Buy shares at the strike price; Short the stock; Receive dividends. Correct answer: Buy shares at the strike price. Why: Call = right to buy. Put = right to sell. Buying a protective put alongside shares is an example of: Options: Eliminating every cost; A guaranteed gain; Hedging downside exposure; Avoiding contract terms. Correct answer: Hedging downside exposure. Why: A put can offset some downside below its strike, but the premium, expiry and other terms matter. pages.description: These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes.
pages.content: The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega Learning notes: The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Summary These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes. Why Greeks matter Greeks are model-based sensitivities to inputs, holding other inputs fixed. Delta describes underlying-price sensitivity; gamma describes a change in delta; theta describes time sensitivity; vega describes implied-volatility sensitivity. Interest rates and dividends can also matter. Finite market moves need not equal a first-order estimate, and different pricing models can produce different values. Delta — directional exposure A delta of 0.50 per share describes an approximate $0.50 option-price change for a $1 underlying move, with other inputs held fixed. For a 100-share contract that is about $50, before gamma and other effects. Some traders use delta as a rough probability shorthand, but it is not a calibrated real-world probability and need not match the model probability of finishing in the money. Gamma — how fast delta changes Gamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. It is often relatively large near the strike close to expiry, depending on volatility and other inputs. Dealer hedging can affect demand, but a chart or open-interest figure alone does not establish dealer positions, required hedges or the cause of a price move. Theta — the ticking clock Theta estimates an option value change as time passes under a model, holding other inputs fixed. State whether the quote is per share or per contract and whether a calendar or trading-day convention is used. Purchased options commonly have negative theta, but realised profit also depends on price, volatility and costs. Selling premium is not a guaranteed collection of that estimate. Vega — volatility sensitivity Vega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility, with other inputs held fixed. Implied volatility can change around earnings, but it need not rise before every release or fall afterwards. A long option can lose despite a favorable underlying move if time decay and a volatility decline offset that move. > Options have several model sensitivities: delta describes underlying-price sensitivity, gamma describes how delta changes with the underlying price, and theta and vega describe time and volatility sensitivities. Hold other model inputs fixed when interpreting each measure. (Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) Key takeaways Delta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability. Gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter. Theta is a model sensitivity; other price changes can offset or exceed it. Vega measures volatility sensitivity; a change in implied volatility is a different quantity. Check your understanding What does theta measure? Options: Directional exposure; Time decay per day; Volatility sensitivity; Interest-rate risk. Correct answer: Time decay per day. Why: Theta is a model estimate of time sensitivity with other inputs held fixed; units and time conventions must be stated. In the lesson example, a 0.50 delta and a $1 underlying rise imply approximately what change per option share, before other effects? Options: $0.10; $0.30; $0.50; $0.90. Correct answer: $0.50. Why: 0.50 × $1 = $0.50 per share, holding other inputs fixed; this is not an event probability. Which event can be followed by a sharp decline in implied volatility? Options: A fixed time every morning; An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty; Every market opening without exception; Every dividend payment without exception. Correct answer: An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty. Why: A sharp post-announcement decline in implied volatility is sometimes called IV crush. It is not confined to earnings and is not inevitable after an announcement. Which Greek measures the rate of change of delta? Options: Vega; Theta; Gamma; Rho. Correct answer: Gamma. Why: Gamma tells you how quickly delta itself changes. Sources OIC — Delta (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta) OIC — Theta (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/theta) OIC — Vega (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/vega) Cboe — options-pricing tools (https://www.cboe.com/education/tools/) Practise this lesson Use $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. pages.content: Defined-Risk Spreads — Verticals & Iron Condors Learning notes: Defined-Risk Spreads — Verticals & Iron Condors Vertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Summary Vertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider. Comparing expiration payoffs A spread combines long and short options. Certain vertical spreads have bounded theoretical payoffs at expiration, unlike an uncovered short call. That comparison does not make spreads universally safe or suitable for beginners. TradeHQ does not execute options spreads; the examples below are worksheet exercises. Bull call spread — a hypothetical example Assume one standard 100-share contract per leg, the same expiration, a $180 long call costing $4 per share and a $185 short call receiving $2. The net debit is $200. With both legs resolved as the expiration payoff assumes, the maximum loss is $200 and the maximum gain is ($185 - $180) × 100 - $200 = $300, before costs. At a $182 expiration price, the $200 intrinsic value offsets the debit for gross break-even. These selected quotes are arithmetic inputs, not current Apple prices or a recommended trade. Iron condor — another payoff structure A short iron condor combines a put credit spread below and a call credit spread above the underlying price. With all four legs intact, its expiration payoff has a maximum gain equal to the net credit when the price lies between the short strikes. Movement beyond the range can produce a loss. Time decay and implied volatility affect its value before expiration; this structure is an example for comparison rather than a preferred trade. A hypothetical sizing worksheet For arithmetic practice, suppose a worksheet assigns 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account to a trade's planned loss budget: that is $1,000-$2,000. These percentages are assumptions, not an institutional standard or a recommendation for a real account. Repeated losses reduce equity, and correlated positions can lose together. The percentage alone does not establish how many trades an account can withstand. What the payoff diagram leaves out Costs and poor fills can change realised results. American-style short options can be assigned before expiration. Exercise or assignment of only one leg can leave stock exposure, particularly near a strike at expiration. A bounded payoff diagram assumes the legs are maintained and resolved together; it is not a guarantee about every account outcome. Closing a spread can reduce remaining expiration exposure but adds execution costs and cannot undo earlier assignment. Worksheet comparison Calculate the bull call example at expiration prices of $175, $182 and $190. Then add an assumed $8 in total costs: the gross outcomes of -$200, $0 and +$300 become -$208, -$8 and +$292. Separately describe what could happen if the short leg were assigned and the stock position remained open. Keep that exposure separate from the intact-spread payoff. (Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) Key takeaways Certain spreads have bounded theoretical expiration payoffs when their legs remain intact. The example's $200 debit and $300 maximum gain exclude costs and additional stock exposure. An iron condor's range-based payoff does not make it a preferred or safe trade. TradeHQ supports spot simulation; options spreads are studied in worksheets. Check your understanding For the intact bull call example, maximum expiration loss before costs is: Options: Unlimited; The width of the spread; The $200 net debit; The strike price. Correct answer: The $200 net debit. Why: Both calls expire worthless below $180, leaving the $200 debit as the gross loss. Costs and separate stock exposure are excluded. An intact short iron condor has its maximum gross expiration gain when the underlying: Options: Rallies sharply beyond the upper wing; Crashes beyond the lower wing; Finishes between the short strikes; Goes to zero. Correct answer: Finishes between the short strikes. Why: The four options expire without intrinsic value between the short strikes, leaving the credit before costs. In the worksheet, 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account equals: Options: $50,000; $25,000; $1,000-$2,000; $100. Correct answer: $1,000-$2,000. Why: 100,000 × 0.01 to 0.02 = $1,000-$2,000. The percentages are illustrative assumptions, not a universal standard. Why can an expiration payoff diagram understate account exposure? Options: It guarantees a profit; It includes all commissions; Assignment of one leg can leave a stock position; Spreads cannot lose. Correct answer: Assignment of one leg can leave a stock position. Why: The intact-spread payoff assumes both legs are resolved together. Assignment can create separate stock exposure and costs. pages.content: Implied Volatility & Trading Around Earnings Learning notes: Implied Volatility & Trading Around Earnings Implied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Summary Implied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility. What implied volatility actually is Implied volatility (IV) is the volatility figure that, plugged into an option pricing model, would produce the option's current market price. It is not a prediction any single person makes — it emerges from the aggregate bids and offers of every participant. Changes can reflect expected uncertainty, demand for protection and risk premiums. IV is model-dependent and need not equal later realised volatility. IV rank vs IV percentile A quoted IV value needs context before comparisons can be interpreted. IV rank commonly compares current IV with the highest and lowest observations over a specified lookback, often 52 weeks, on a 0–100 scale. A constant series has no high-low range, so the usual calculation is undefined. Under one common convention, IV percentile is the fraction of observations below the current value over a stated lookback. Check the provider's treatment of equal observations and the chosen series. Neither an IV-rank threshold nor an IV-percentile threshold establishes a buy or sell rule. Compare the chosen lookback, option expiry, price source and costs before interpreting either measure. The earnings trap Implied volatility often rises before earnings and can fall sharply afterwards. A trader can be directionally correct and still lose on a long option if the volatility drop and time decay outweigh the price move. Comparing hypothetical earnings payoffs In a paper worksheet, compare hypothetical long-premium and defined-risk premium-selling structures around earnings to see how direction, implied volatility and the size of the actual move interact. TradeHQ does not price these structures. Avoid treating volatility selling as inherently safer; short premium can carry substantial risk. Practice loop For a historical study, record dated option quotes and implied-volatility observations from an options-data source before and after an earnings announcement. Keep the expiry, strike and data methodology consistent, and record price changes as well as volatility changes. TradeHQ does not supply an options chain or IV-rank data. A small sample can illustrate mechanisms without establishing a reliable trading edge. (Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) Key takeaways IV is inferred from option prices under a model; it can differ from future realised volatility. IV rank contextualises today's IV against the last 12 months. IV crush after earnings can turn a correct directional bet into a loss. Elevated implied volatility changes the payoff profile of premium-selling strategies, but higher premiums also reflect higher expected uncertainty and risk. Check your understanding Under the lesson's 52-week high-low convention, what does IV rank of 80 describe? Options: IV is at 80%; IV is toward the upper end of its observed range; IV is near a 12-month low; 80% of options are profitable. Correct answer: IV is toward the upper end of its observed range. Why: IV rank describes relative location within a specified high-low range, not the fraction of days below the current value. Why can a long option lose even if the price moves in the expected direction after earnings? Options: Because options never follow the underlying; A drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain; Because earnings cancel the contract; Because all options are illiquid. Correct answer: A drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain. Why: Option value depends on more than direction; implied volatility and time value can change sharply after earnings. What does a high IV rank tell you? Options: A premium-selling trade is guaranteed to work; Current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range; The stock must fall; The next move will be small. Correct answer: Current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range. Why: IV rank is context about relative option pricing, not a standalone buy or sell signal. Implied volatility is: Options: Historical vol over 30 days; An exchange forecast; The volatility that makes model = market price; The stock's beta. Correct answer: The volatility that makes model = market price. Why: IV is the vol input that reconciles a pricing model with the live option price.
